title: ROSA: A Robotics Foundation Model Serving System for Robot Factories
authors: Wenqi Jiang; Jason Clemons; Rowland O’Flaherty; Hugo Hadfield; Alperen Değirmenci; Shuran Song; Yashraj Narang; Christos Kozyrakis
abstract: Robotics foundation models (RFMs) are making general-purpose robots increasingly practical for factory deployments. While RFM serving systems are central to this vision, existing systems are largely shaped by a single-robot, single-model assumption: inference is treated as an edge-computing problem handled by an on-robot or dedicated nearby GPU, and the serving objective is to minimize the latency of a single action model. In this paper, we propose ROSA, an RFM serving system for robot factories designed around three key principles. First, ROSA adopts shared GPU-pool serving, allowing a fleet of robots to access powerful server-class GPUs over the network in order to improve inference performance, battery duration, and GPU utilization. Second, ROSA provides a robotics-aware programming abstraction and system design that supports multi-model pipelines, per-task performance requirements, and failure handling. Third, ROSA uses factory-objective-driven scheduling to maximize SLO-qualified factory productivity rather than minimizing individual request latency. We implement ROSA on top of Ray Serve for distributed orchestration, with vLLM, PyTorch, and JAX as model-serving backends, and evaluate it on both real robots and synthetic large-scale workloads. The results show that ROSA improves factory productivity by up to 12.06x over conventional dedicated serving systems.

title: Inqeduagent: Adaptive AI Learning Partners with Gaussian Process Augmentation
authors: Wen-Xi Yang; Tian-Fang Zhao; Guan Liu
source_name: Asia Conference on Machine Learning and Computing (ACMLC)
abstract: Collaborative partnerships play a crucial role in inquiry-oriented education. However, most learning partners are currently assigned through experience-driven heuristics or rule-based machine assistants, which often result in limited knowledge expansion and low adaptability. To address these challenges, this study introduces InqEduAgent, an LLM-empowered generative agent framework designed to simulate and select adaptive learning partners for inquiry-based learning. InqEduAgent integrates a Gaussian process-augmented matching mechanism to model the cognitive and evaluative characteristics of learners, allowing adaptive partner selection based on prior knowledge patterns. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that InqEduAgent consistently achieves superior performance across diverse learning scenarios and large language model configurations. This study advances human-AI collaborative learning by enabling intelligent pairing between human- and AI-based learning partners, and contributes to adaptive user modeling and personalized recommendation within Web-based educational environments.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-DRIVEN ENHANCEMENT OF HUMAN CAPITAL INVESTMENT ATTRACTION MECHANISMS
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This article explores the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in enhancing mechanisms for attracting investments in human capital within the context of the digital economy. The study examines theoretical foundations, including the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, to explain the strategic value of human capital as a key driver of sustainable economic development. Particular attention is devoted to AI-driven solutions such as machine learning, predictive analytics, natural language processing, generative AI, big data analytics, and reinforcement learning that improve decision-making in human capital investment planning and resource allocation.

title: Organizing Immersion: A Sociomaterial Study of AI-Driven Non-Wearable Interactive Environments
authors: C.Y. Wang; Zhuojun Li; Y W Su
abstract: Sociomaterial research has fundamentally reshaped how scholars understand the constitutive entanglement of technology and organizing. Yet, despite its ontological commitments, existing empirical studies have largely examined technologies that remain experientially distinguishable as bounded artifacts—such as tools, systems, or platforms. This paper examines what happens when this implicit artifact-centered anchoring no longer holds. Even studies that emphasize fluidity, performativity, or becoming typically rely on empirical settings in which technologies retain identifiable material forms, interfaces, or systems that can be analytically foregrounded. Drawing on a qualitative, multi-site study of AI-driven, non-wearable immersive environments in experiential service settings, this study advances a design-oriented framework in which technology operates as a responsive environment rather than a discrete artifact. Centered on immersive narrative dining, the framework articulates an end-to-end automated pipeline that integrates multimodal generative AI, spatial computing, and real-time sensor-driven interaction, offering a replicable model for the design of next-generation experiential services. Our findings identify three shifts that challenge artifact-centered applications of sociomaterial theory: (1) organizational action emerges through environmental participation rather than artifact interaction; (2) managerial control is enacted through continuous calibration of environmental responsiveness rather than governance of stable systems; and (3) organizational routines stabilize as adaptive, improvisational patterns co-evolving with responsive environments. Theoretically, we argue that AI-driven immersive environments represent a boundary condition for artifact-centered sociomaterial theorizing and call for an extension that accounts for responsive sociotechnical environments. We contribute to Technology and Innovation Management research by showing how innovation increasingly involves designing and governing generative environments rather than implementing discrete technological artifacts, thereby reframing core assumptions about control, value creation, and organizational capability in AI-enabled contexts.

title: Intelligent Datacenter Networks: Integrating Software-Defined Networking, Artificial Intelligence, and Autonomous Network Operations
source_name: International Journal of Advance Industrial Engineering
abstract: The rapid growth of cloud-native applications, large-scale artificial intelligence workloads, and latency-sensitive edge services has placed unprecedented demands on datacenter network infrastructure. In response, the networking industry is converging around three transformative paradigms: Software-Defined Networking (SDN), which decouples control logic from forwarding hardware to enable centralized programmability; Artificial Intelligence for networking (AI4Net), which applies machine learning to traffic optimization, anomaly detection, and capacity planning; and Autonomous Network Operations (ANO), which aspires to closed-loop, self-configuring, self-optimizing, and self-healing network management with minimal human intervention. This paper presents a comprehensive, integrated survey of these three paradigms and their synergistic convergence in modern datacenter environments. We begin by examining the architectural evolution of SDN from early OpenFlow-centric designs to contemporary intent-driven, multi-layer control platforms that govern network, compute, and storage resources holistically. We then survey AI-driven networking techniques, including deep reinforcement learning for traffic engineering, graph neural networks for topology-aware optimization, transformer-based models for network telemetry analysis, and generative AI for configuration synthesis. Next, we analyze autonomous network operations frameworks, covering closed-loop automation architectures, digital twin-based validation, formal verification of network invariants, and trust and explainability requirements for human-machine teaming. We further investigate cross-cutting concerns including programmable data planes, network security automation, multi-domain orchestration, and energy-efficient networking. Finally, we identify open research challenges and chart future directions toward fully intelligent, self-driving datacenter networks. By synthesizing insights from over 80 references spanning academic research, industry practice, and standards development, this article provides a unified reference for researchers, architects, and practitioners working at the intersection of networking, AI, and autonomous systems.

title: Editorial: Digital transformation in transport and logistics
abstract: The digital transformation of transport and logistics has moved from a strategic aspiration to an operational necessity. The intellectual origins of this shift trace back to the Industry 4.0 initiative of the early 2010s, when the integration of cyber-physical systems placed digital-physical convergence at the center of industrial strategy (Kagermann, 2013; Sullivan and Kern, 2021). For much of that decade, however, the practical distance between vision and reality remained wide.What narrowed this gap was the rapid development of enabling technologies. Internet of Things (IoT) devices, cloud computing, machine learning and autonomous systems such as Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) and warehouse robots moved from experimental settings into live logistics operations (Fottner et al., 2021; Fragapane et al., 2021; Escherle et al., 2023; Lam et al., 2024). A growing body of research has documented the resulting improvements in visibility, asset utilization and decision-making capability across the value chain. Industry 4.0 has positioned digital technologies as central enablers of this transformation (Barreto et al., 2017). IoT devices now provide real-time visibility into the movement and condition of goods across extended transport chains (Barreto et al., 2017; Feng and Ye, 2021). Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning algorithms support demand forecasting, route optimization and predictive maintenance (Hoffmann et al., 2022; Nitsche et al., 2024). Cloud computing and digital platforms facilitate the integration of fragmented logistics ecosystems by connecting shippers, carriers, terminal operators and end customers through shared data environments (Winkelhaus and Grosse, 2020).The 2020s then introduced a different kind of pressure. The COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent geopolitical disruptions revealed the fragility of efficiency-optimized but resilience-deficient logistics networks. Contact restrictions, acute labor shortages and simultaneous demand shocks forced many organizations to compress years of planned digitalization into months (Ivanov, 2021; Hellweg et al., 2023). The resulting recalibration was structural. End-to-end supply chain visibility and data-driven decision-making became operational necessities rather than competitive advantages, and the need to collect, integrate and act on operational data intensified across the industry.The consequence is a rapidly growing number of interfaces among physical assets, digital tools and humans throughout the transport and logistics value chain. Figure 1 illustrates them as a three-level architecture: at the physical level, physical assets (e.g. vehicles and facilities), field and IoT devices generate ongoing data about what is happening in the logistics system; at the digital level, these data are ingested, stored, integrated and exchanged across systems through application programming interfaces (APIs) and related system connections, where they support event management, interoperability and consistent digital representations of operations; these representations provide the basis for data-driven analytics and decision-making at the analytical level, such as diagnostic assessments of current system states, predictive analytics for future developments, reality-based scenario analysis and higher-level decision support. The analytical outputs, in turn, move downward to shape physical behavior through accurate and reliable control signals (Albrecht et al., 2024). This bidirectional architecture has considerable productive potential. However, realizing it requires ensuring that digital systems can accurately capture the complexity of the physical world and that analytical outputs can be effectively translated into operational decisions.This special issue of Logistics Research was designed to address these dual challenges. It invited analytical, conceptual, empirical, experimental and optimization contributions that advance the understanding of digital and technological interfaces in transport and logistics at both the technological and the organizational-planning levels. In particular, the integration of digital technologies into physical assets and processes, as well as the application of data-driven analytical methods for supply chain decision-making, were identified as areas of primary interest. The two contributions of this special issue, Wehner (2026) and Doege (2026), address two essential and complementary dimensions of this transformation though different in scope and methodology: the physical implementation of autonomous technologies and the analytical use of network data for resilience.Digital interfaces in transport and logistics differ fundamentally in the nature of the problems they address and the level at which those problems arise. To position this heterogeneity, we propose a two-dimensional conceptual framework that distinguishes between the nature of the digital interface, depending on whether digital technologies primarily sense, translate and control physical assets (physical-digital interface) or act on digital representations of them (analytical-digital interface). This framework also distinguishes between the levels of analysis at which challenges and decisions arise for specific operations and technologies or across network-level coordination. These two dimensions are analytically necessary because operational and network-level challenges differ in scope, time horizon and coordination requirements, while the two interface types raise distinct technological and organizational issues. Table 1 maps this space through selected examples. The two contributions in this special issue occupy distinct positions within this space, as discussed in Section 2.3.This framework reflects observations drawn from a broader community, including discussions within the production, logistics and transportation research community, including exchanges at the 7th Interdisciplinary Conference on Production, Logistics and Traffic (ICPLT), held in Darmstadt in March 2025. These discussions covered the full spectrum from physical automation to network-level analytics across rail freight, road transport, maritime logistics, urban delivery and terminal operations.Physical-digital interfaces refer to the points at which physical assets (e.g. robots, vehicles, containers and terminal equipment) become readable by digital systems and at which digital instructions are translated into physical behavior. Lee et al. (2015) proposed a five-layer architecture for cyber-physical systems that precisely captures this bidirectional flow from physical sensing to digital action, spanning connection, conversion, cyber, cognition and configuration. At both the operational and the network levels, the challenges are primarily technological. For example, how can an autonomous system reliably perceive and act in a dynamic, unstructured environment, and how can the resulting information be safely shared and made interoperable across various systems (Kembro et al., 2017; Fottner et al., 2021)? Beyond the technical dimension, physical-digital interfaces raise equally significant organizational questions. The introduction of autonomous systems into existing workflows requires process re-engineering, personnel retraining and often fundamental rethinking of task allocation between humans and machines (Cichosz et al., 2020; Hellweg et al., 2023).Analytical-digital interfaces are the boundaries between digital representations of the real world and the computational methods used to extract useful information from them. The central challenge here is epistemological: What data and metrics are sufficient for effective decision-making, and how much network visibility is actually needed? The growing availability of various data sources has considerably expanded the scope of these interfaces. Yet data availability alone does not guarantee usefulness. Supply chain networks are characterized by information asymmetries, data quality issues and coordination failures, and autonomous entities typically make decisions based on local and incomplete information, so that what any single actor can reliably infer and influence remains limited (Delfmann et al., 2018; Fottner et al., 2021). Therefore, the practical value of digital analysis at this interface depends on whether data-driven decision rules and performance indicators can be translated into operationally feasible actions in specific organizational and network contexts.The two contributions in this special issue occupy complementary positions within the framework proposed above. Together, they illustrate how digital transformation in transport and logistics unfolds through two distinct but interconnected modes: the physical implementation of autonomous technologies and the analytical use of network-level data for resilience-oriented decision-making.Wehner (2026) are positioned at the physical-digital interface on the operational level. Their empirical study investigates the integration of automation and digital technologies in air cargo logistics through the empirical testing of the O3dyn pallet transport robot at Munich Airport. This study documents a ten-day real-world trial in which the robot's performance was assessed across multiple transport scenarios, with data collected on travel times, load weights, manual interventions and operational challenges.Doege (2026) are positioned at the analytical-digital interface on the network level, addressing one concrete analytical question: How can supply chain networks be made more resilient against disruption propagation, and how much network visibility is actually required for this purpose? Using agent-based modeling combined with a susceptible-infected-recovered epidemiological framework, the authors simulate disruption cascades across ten real-world supply chain networks and evaluate five node-selection strategies derived from social network analysis metrics.Digital transformation in transport and logistics has moved past the stage of technology demonstration into a period that requires empirically grounded and organizationally sensitive research. The two-dimensional framework proposed here offers a means of positioning and connecting contributions across this field. The papers in this special issue represent two reference points in that space. Viewed through this framework, their respective scopes point directly toward the most consequential open research directions. Yet the scope of the present issue necessarily remains selective. Some important dimensions are not addressed directly.The interfaces among the physical, digital and analytical levels are not independent. Digital twins represent the most developed form of this interdependence, functioning simultaneously as physical-digital synchronization mechanisms and as analytical simulation environments (Tao et al., 2018; Fottner et al., 2021). While a growing body of research has begun to explore their potential in logistics and supply chain management, this dimension falls outside the scope of the present issue and warrants continued attention, particularly in multi-actor and cross-modal settings where the integration of operational data streams with network-level decision support remains technically and organizationally demanding.Furthermore, the rapid emergence of generative AI and large language models represents the most visible frontier. Applications such as natural language interfaces for freight procurement, generative scenario planning for supply chain risk and AI-assisted coordination across carrier networks demonstrate the remarkable potential of these disruptive technologies in logistics decision-making. While these applications are situated at the analytical-digital interface, they also introduce new challenges regarding model interpretability and human oversight. As the submission timelines preceded this period, these developments are not addressed in this special issue. However, they do deserve more focused attention in future research.The contributions in this special issue encourage further inquiry at the intersection of physical automation and network intelligence, advancing both the technological and the organizational foundations of digital transformation in transport and logistics.During the preparation of this work, the authors used Grammarly and Claude in the writing process to improve the readability and language of the manuscript. After using this tool/service, the authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.The Guest Editors wish to thank all authors who responded to the call for papers, the anonymous reviewers whose expertise ensured the quality of the review process and the Editor-in-Chief of Logistics Research for the opportunity to organize this special issue. They also wish to acknowledge the organizers and participants of the 7th Interdisciplinary Conference on Production, Logistics and Traffic, whose presentations and discussions on digital transformation in transport and logistics provided a broader intellectual context for this special issue.

For example, how can an autonomous system reliably perceive and act in a dynamic, unstructured environment, and how can the resulting information be safely shared and made interoperable across various systems (Kembro et al., 2017; Fottner et al., 2021)? Beyond the technical dimension, physical-digital interfaces raise equally significant organizational questions. The introduction of autonomous systems into existing workflows requires process re-engineering, personnel retraining and often fundamental rethinking of task allocation between humans and machines (Cichosz et al., 2020; Hellweg et al., 2023).Analytical-digital interfaces are the boundaries between digital representations of the real world and the computational methods used to extract useful information from them. The central challenge here is epistemological: What data and metrics are sufficient for effective decision-making, and how much network visibility is actually needed? The growing availability of various data sources has considerably expanded the scope of these interfaces. Yet data availability alone does not guarantee usefulness. Supply chain networks are characterized by information asymmetries, data quality issues and coordination failures, and autonomous entities typically make decisions based on local and incomplete information, so that what any single actor can reliably infer and influence remains limited (Delfmann et al., 2018; Fottner et al., 2021). Therefore, the practical value of digital analysis at this interface depends on whether data-driven decision rules and performance indicators can be translated into operationally feasible actions in specific organizational and network contexts.The two contributions in this special issue occupy complementary positions within the framework proposed above. Together, they illustrate how digital transformation in transport and logistics unfolds through two distinct but interconnected modes: the physical implementation of autonomous technologies and the analytical use of network-level data for resilience-oriented decision-making.Wehner (2026) are positioned at the physical-digital interface on the operational level. Their empirical study investigates the integration of automation and digital technologies in air cargo logistics through the empirical testing of the O3dyn pallet transport robot at Munich Airport. The two-dimensional framework proposed here offers a means of positioning and connecting contributions across this field. The papers in this special issue represent two reference points in that space. Viewed through this framework, their respective scopes point directly toward the most consequential open research directions. Yet the scope of the present issue necessarily remains selective. Some important dimensions are not addressed directly.The interfaces among the physical, digital and analytical levels are not independent. Digital twins represent the most developed form of this interdependence, functioning simultaneously as physical-digital synchronization mechanisms and as analytical simulation environments (Tao et al., 2018; Fottner et al., 2021). While these applications are situated at the analytical-digital interface, they also introduce new challenges regarding model interpretability and human oversight. title: ACCOUNTING AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
abstract: Accounting and Artificial Intelligence: Transforming Financial Reporting, Auditing, and Decision-Making in the Digital Age presents a comprehensive exploration of how artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the accounting profession. Authored by Ahmad Omar Hardan, this book positions AI not merely as a technological tool but as a transformative force that redefines the very essence of accounting practice—from transaction processing and financial reporting to auditing, taxation, and strategic decision-making. Through its systematic integration of AI technologies—including machine learning, natural language processing, robotic process automation, and generative AI—with core accounting functions, this volume demonstrates how financial professionals can harness intelligent systems to enhance accuracy, efficiency, and insight. The book traces the evolution of accounting from manual bookkeeping through the digital revolution to the current AI-driven paradigm, emphasizing the potential of these technologies to address perennial challenges such as fraud detection, regulatory compliance, and real-time financial analysis. It examines the strategic frameworks, operational structures, and ethical governance systems that underpin successful AI adoption in accounting, offering a benchmark for firms and institutions worldwide. With a forward-looking lens, the author articulates a vision of accounting where intelligent automation complements human expertise—where technology becomes a catalyst for deeper analytical insight, strategic advisory, and sustainable value creation. The book delves into how strategic alignment of AI with core accounting functions—from bookkeeping and financial reporting to auditing, taxation, and management accounting—enhances accuracy, efficiency, and strategic value creation for both organizations and stakeholders. At its core, this work situates AI within a broader transformation of the accounting profession—one that reconciles technological capability with professional judgment and ethical responsibility. Through empirical analysis and conceptual exploration, it demonstrates how AI-powered systems translate vast amounts of financial data into actionable insights, predictive analytics, and real-time decision support. The study highlights key operational frameworks, from automated transaction processing and continuous auditing to AI-driven risk assessment and fraud detection systems. Ahmad Omar Hardan elucidates how regulatory environments, institutional innovation, and socioeconomic contexts converge to support the adoption of AI in accounting. The narrative underscores that AI is not merely a technological upgrade but a fundamental reimagining of how financial information is captured, processed, analyzed, and communicated. It also addresses the multi-dimensional challenges—regulatory, ethical, technical, and organizational—that must be navigated to ensure that AI adoption yields tangible and responsible outcomes. It argues that an integrated approach—balancing innovation, transparency, and professional skepticism—offers a replicable model for accounting firms, corporations, and regulators worldwide. title: Large Language Models as non-Player Characters in Massively Multiplayer Online Role-Playing Games: A Systematic Scoping Review
abstract: This project is a systematic scoping review (built on a systematic, multi-database search) examining the use of large language models (LLMs) and generative AI to power non-player characters (NPCs) in video games, with a specific focus on the demands of massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs). Traditional NPCs rely on static, scripted dialogue, which players consistently identify as an immersion barrier; LLMs offer context-aware, memory-aware, and socially flexible interaction, but their deployment at the scale, persistence, and adversarial exposure of an MMORPG raises unresolved questions of capability, player impact, engineering feasibility, and safety. The purpose of this review is to map and critically appraise the existing evidence base so that researchers and developers can understand what is currently demonstrated, what remains unproven, and what is required before responsible large-scale deployment. The review addresses four pre-specified questions, organised around a PECO framework (Population: MMORPG players and NPC systems; Exposure: LLM-driven or generative-AI NPCs; Comparator: scripted or rule-based NPC baselines; Outcomes below). (1) Capability: what can LLM-driven NPCs reliably do beyond scripted dialogue, including memory, social reasoning, action selection, and multi-agent interaction? (2) Player outcomes: do LLM-driven NPCs measurably improve immersion, engagement, believability, or usability, and under what conditions? (3) Systems constraints: which architecture patterns best bind LLM outputs to authoritative game rules, latency budgets, and content-safety constraints? (4) Risk and governance: what is required to mitigate hallucination-driven false affordances, prompt-injection exploits, and bias or toxicity harms at MMO scale? Eligible sources are peer-reviewed studies, preprints, theses, and grey-literature/industry reports (January 2020 – February 2026) reporting on generative AI or LLMs applied to game NPCs or autonomous game agents, with a retrievable methodology and available in English. Eight databases and repositories were searched (ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, PubMed, Google Scholar, GDC Vault, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, and targeted industry repositories including NVIDIA and Inworld AI), supplemented by citation chaining of two anchor reviews. Records are screened in two stages against the eligibility criteria, data are extracted using a pre-specified structured form, risk of bias is assessed with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018), and certainty of evidence is appraised with a modified GRADE approach. The primary synthesis is a structured qualitative narrative organised by the four questions; quantitative synthesis is limited to studies reporting extractable comparative statistics, with the standardised mean difference (Hedges' g) as the pre-specified effect measure. Expected outcomes: the review is anticipated to show that LLM-driven NPCs are technically feasible and show directional promise for player engagement, but that the evidence base is sparse, heterogeneous, and dominated by small prototype studies and industry reports, yielding low overall certainty. We expect player-facing quantitative evidence to be extremely limited (likely a single study with combinable statistics, giving a small-to-moderate but non-significant effect with wide confidence intervals), latency and conversational failure modes to emerge as the dominant deployment barriers, and hybrid constraint-layer architectures, governed memory systems, and adversarial security testing (against prompt injection and bias/toxicity) to be identified as critical engineering and governance requirements. The intended contribution is the first PRISMA-aligned synthesis of LLM-NPC evidence framed for MMORPG deployment, alongside a research agenda calling for pre-registered, adequately powered, multi-site player evaluations. This registration is retrospective: the literature search and data extraction were conducted prior to registration. It is being deposited to provide a transparent, time-stamped record of the review's objectives, eligibility criteria, search strategy, extraction fields, and synthesis methods.

title: A Decision Support System for Rapid Deployment of Emergency Healthcare Facilities for Infectious Disease Using Augmented Large Language Models
authors: Guanying Huang; Shenghua Zhou; S Thomas Ng; Hongzhe Yue; Dezhi Li
abstract: The emergency healthcare facilities for infectious disease deployment (EHFIDD) is a crucial measure to alleviate the pressure placed on healthcare systems by public health emergencies caused by infectious outbreaks. However, the rapid EHFIDD involves short timelines, stringent quality requirements, and numerous decision points. Therefore, it is urgent to develop a decision support system (DSS) capable of guiding a scientific and efficient deployment process from site selection to final delivery within a limited timeframe. Previous studies have primarily developed rule-based and pretrained DSS for the rapid EHFIDD, which heavily relied on predefined knowledge and manual configuration, resulting in limited efficiency and scalability. To address this limitation, this study used an augmented large language model (LLM) to develop and deploy a DSS prototype for rapid EHFIDD, simultaneously achieving high development efficiency and reliable decision-making performance. Specifically, this study established an LLM-enabled knowledge graph (KG) development method tailored for EHFIDD-related standards; developed a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based approach to augment six recent LLMs using EHFIDD-KG; and proposed a comprehensive evaluation system for DSS performance, including accuracy, traceability, and relevance. Results show that (1) medium-scale LLMs achieve more augmentation from EHFIDD-KG than ultralarge LLMs; (2) the augmentation is more pronounced in answering open-ended questions than closed-ended ones; (3) the augmented LLMs achieve average improvements of 0.20, 0.40, and 0.21 in accuracy, traceability, and relevance over the original model; and (4) KG containing image information outperforms text-only KG with average gains of 0.08, 0.05, and 0.12 in accuracy, traceability, and relevance. Finally, the DSS’ robustness and generalizability are discussed, alongside its theoretical contributions, managerial implications, and human-centric governance for deployment safety. This study provides a systematic and reliable methodology for DSS development in rapid EHFIDD contexts and offers a novel technical pathway for enabling explainable LLM applications in emergency engineering domains.

title: Covering the Unseen: Information Demand Coverage Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Bingxue Zhang; Jianying Jia; Feida Zhu
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically treats context selection as ranking chunks against a single query embedding. This assumption breaks down for complex queries, such as multi-hop or ambiguous questions, where top-k selection tends to over-cover one semantic aspect while ignoring critical sub-questions. We propose GeoRAG, which recasts context selection as Information Demand Coverage Optimization. GeoRAG builds a multi-dimensional demand distribution through diverse sub-query generation and reverse-validation weighting, then selects context by minimizing the Sinkhorn-Wasserstein distance between this demand distribution and the coverage of the selected set. The resulting demand-weighted facility-location objective is monotone submodular, giving a $1-1/e$ greedy guarantee, which we approximate with a Sinkhorn-based marginal-gain surrogate. The method is unsupervised, training-free, and retrieval-agnostic. We further show that single-point, query-proximity scorers cannot cover multi-modal demands, exposing a structural limit of ranking-based selection. On six open-domain QA benchmarks, GeoRAG improves exact match (EM) by +6.5 to +7.5 points over top-k truncation (up to +9.7 on HotpotQA and ASQA) and outperforms strong baselines including MMR, DPP, BGE-Reranker, SMART-RAG, and AdaGReS, with stable gains across context budgets and sub-query generators.

title: KernelSight-LM: A Kernel-Level LLM Inference Simulator
authors: Xiteng Yao; Taeho Kim; Hengzhi Pei; Xinle Liu; Kyle Ulrich; Leonard Lausen; Ashish Khetan; Xiang Song; George Karypis; Martin Herbordt
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) move into production serving, practitioners must rapidly evaluate inference performance across diverse hardware, models, and serving parameters to meet cost and latency targets. However, the end-to-end behavior of LLMs couples serving-layer policies with low-level GPU kernel execution and rapidly evolving architectures, forcing slow, deployment-specific benchmarking that is hard to generalize. We present KernelSight-LM, a fine-grained inference simulator that models token-level execution and produces kernel-level latency breakdowns. It decomposes each serving step into a roofline kernel model with a learned efficiency term, a communication model, and a host-overhead model, composed through a discrete-event scheduler that also captures mechanisms like prefix caching and continuous batching. KernelSight-LM offers two prediction tiers that trade target-GPU data for accuracy. The cross-generation tier uses no target-GPU measurements, only hardware specifications and kernel microbenchmarks from previously profiled GPUs, and predicts per-kernel latency on an unseen GPU generation to 12.1% error, a 1.8x improvement over the roofline baseline (22.0%). A second target-measured tier adds one model-agnostic kernel-microbenchmark sweep on the target GPU, sharpening per-kernel error to 3.8%, a 7.3x improvement over a comparable baseline (27.7%). Both tiers require far less target-GPU data than the prior systems they extend. In our simulator, these predictions yield end-to-end median (p50) errors across six model families of 15.4%, 12.8%, and 3.0% (TTFT, TPOT, throughput) in the cross-generation tier and 14.3%, 6.2%, and 2.7% in the target-measured tier, matching dedicated profiling tools while collecting far less on-device data. Beyond prediction, its kernel-level bottleneck breakdowns support hardware/software co-design and capacity planning.

title: The Spatial Footprint of Artificial Intelligence: Evaluating the Friction Between Fast-Tracked Digital Infrastructure and Local Land-Use Governance in Italy
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The generative AI boom has turned data centres from invisible utilities into one of the most land-, power- and water-intensive building types of the early twenty-first century. Planning theory, however, still tends to treat them through the dematerialising language of “the cloud.” This paper examines the institutional friction that the AI build-out has produced in Italy, where the national state and sub-national governments moved in opposite directions within a single quarter of 2026. Law Decree 21/2026 (Article 8) created a fast-tracked single national authorisation procedure (procedimento unico nazionale) with a binding statutory deadline of ten months, extendable to thirteen. Its purpose was to capture mobile hyperscale capital before it relocated to other European markets. Within weeks, the Lombardy region reasserted territorial control through Regional Law 11/2026, which routes large projects into supra-municipal planning agreements, requires wasteheat recovery audits, and imposes equalisation and compensation levies on built surface. We read these instruments against the actual reorganisation of Italy’s data-centre geography: the saturated Milan inference cluster, the brownfield conversion of the former Galileo Ferraris thermoelectric plant at Trino in Piedmont, and the subsea-cable and renewables story now unfolding as a “Data Center Valley” in Puglia. AI infrastructure, we argue, exposes a territorial blind spot in planning practice. We develop that argument through two distinctions: between the spatial logics of AI training and AI inference, and between data centres as engines of industrial requalification and as instruments of territorial extraction. The governance question is not whether to authorise these facilities. It is how to convert a highly automated, low-employment, resource-hungry industry, one that runs on accelerated corporate timelines, into durable local public value. That conversion requires a shift from reactive zoning toward proactive territorial equalisation.

title: Digitized and AI-Assisted Scoring of Cognitive Assessments in ALS and Neurodegenerative Diseases: A Scoping Review of Consistency, Reliability, and Cross-Site Applicability
authors: Indu Navar Bingham; Anusha Rao; Natalia Luchkina; Sharon Abrahams; Ammar Al‐Chalabi
abstract: Background. Standardized cognitive assessment across clinical sites remains a major challenge in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and related neurodegenerative diseases. The Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioral ALS Screen (ECAS) is the most validated and widely-used ALS-specific cognitive assessment tool, yet paper-and-pencil manual scoring introduces inter-rater variability that can significantly limit reliability and reproducibility in multi-site clinical trials. Digitized administration and artificial intelligence-assisted scoring may improve consistency and scalability, but the current landscape across ALS and related diseases has not been systematically mapped.Objective. To map existing evidence on digitized and AI-assisted scoring of cognitive assessments in ALS and other neurodegenerative and neuroinflammatory diseases, with emphasis on inter-rater reliability and cross-site consistency.Methods. We conducted a comprehensive scoping review following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Eligible studies evaluated neuropsychological or cognitive assessment tools using automated, computerized, digital, or AI-assisted scoring in ALS and related conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, dementia, and neuroinflammatory disease. An initial broad PubMed search was refined to focus on records explicitly addressing automated or AI-assisted scoring in titles and abstracts. Records were loaded into Rayyan for independent blinded review by three reviewers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion until consensus was reached. Data were extracted using standardized templates.Results. The initial search identified 1,503 records and was refined to 168 records. After duplicate removal, 166 records underwent title, abstract, and full-text screening against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Seven primary studies met inclusion criteria: two in multiple sclerosis, two in the Alzheimer's disease continuum, and three in dementia or mild cognitive impairment. AI and digital approaches included tablet-based digitization with automated scoring, convolutional neural networks, and large language models. All seven studies reported high agreement with human or paper-based reference standards. No primary study evaluating AI-assisted scoring of the ECAS or ALS-specific cognitive screens was identified.Conclusions. This review maps AI-assisted and digitized cognitive assessment scoring in neurodegenerative and neuroinflammatory diseases. Findings reveal a critical gap in ALS-specific cognitive tools and ECAS scoring. Methodological approaches from related diseases, especially automated scoring of verbal and written responses, may inform future development of standardized AI-assisted ECAS protocols. Such tools could improve consistency, reliability, and scalability across multi-site ALS clinical trials.

title: Patent Analysis of Providing Services Related to Item Delivery via 3D Manufacturing on Demand: US9898776B2
source_name: Poornaprajna International Journal of Basic & Applied Sciences (PIJBAS)
abstract: Purpose: To systematically examine the patent and evaluate its technological, strategic, and commercial significance in the emerging field of on-demand digital manufacturing. The study aims to investigate how the patented invention integrates customer ordering, additive manufacturing, and delivery management into a unified ecosystem that enhances customization, reduces inventory dependency, and improves supply-chain efficiency. Furthermore, the article seeks to assess the patent’s innovation potential, business value, societal impact, and future opportunities through structured analytical frameworks, thereby contributing to knowledge creation in the domains of 3D manufacturing, e-commerce, and technology-driven logistics. Methodology: This study adopts an exploratory qualitative research approach to systematically analyze the selected patent. Relevant data were collected from open-access sources, including Google Search, Google Patents, Google Scholar, and AI-powered GPT tools, and were subsequently organized and interpreted according to the study objectives. Structured analytical frameworks such as SWOC and ABCDEF were applied to generate meaningful insights into the patent's technological, strategic, and commercial significance. Results & Analysis: The analysis reveals that the patent “Providing Services Related to Item Delivery via 3D Manufacturing on Demand” introduces a transformative framework that integrates customer ordering, digital design management, distributed 3D manufacturing, and intelligent delivery services into a unified ecosystem. The results indicate significant advantages in terms of inventory reduction, mass customization, supply-chain optimization, localized production, and enhanced customer satisfaction, while also highlighting challenges related to intellectual property protection, cybersecurity, quality assurance, and infrastructure requirements. Overall, the study demonstrates that the patent possesses strong technological innovation, substantial commercial potential, and strategic relevance for the future development of Industry 4.0, smart manufacturing, and on-demand digital commerce systems. Originality & Values: The originality of this patent analysis lies in its unique integration of customer ordering, digital design management, on-demand 3D manufacturing, and intelligent delivery coordination within a single end-to-end ecosystem. The study adds scholarly value by demonstrating how digital inventories, distributed manufacturing networks, and mass customization can transform traditional production and supply-chain models into flexible, customer-centric systems. Furthermore, the patent offers significant technological, commercial, and societal value by supporting sustainable manufacturing, reducing inventory dependence, and enabling next-generation Industry 4.0 business models. Type of Paper: Case Study-based Exploratory Research.

title: An ambiguity taxonomy for evaluating large language model performance on clinical registry abstraction: a multi-site prospective study
authors: James Matheson; Betsy Castillo; Andrew Y. Shin; David Scheinker
abstract: Objective: To evaluate large language model (LLM) performance on unprocessed electronic medical record (EMR) data for clinical registry abstraction. Methods: We evaluated LLM performance answering registry questions for the American College of Cardiology National Cardiovascular Data Registry (ACC NCDR). In a pilot study at an academic medical center, the model identified candidate data sources for each registry question and experienced abstractors used these results to define question-specific document sets. In a validation study at a second center with a second ACC NCDR registry, the LLM answered questions using the question-specific document sets. Before reviewing any output, two abstractors independently established the ground truth and assigned each question to one of six categories, ordered by the ambiguity and clinical reasoning required to resolve it: Medication/Event Flag, Binary Clinical Presence, Administrative, Quantitative Laboratory/Physiologic, Clinical Interpretation, and Event Timing. Results: The analytical sample comprised 9,430 abstractor answers reconciled to 4,715 consensus answers (501 pilot; 4,214 validation). In the pilot, candidate data sources per question averaged between 14.6 (SD 13.9) for demographics and 89.2 (SD 56.1) for history and risk factors. In validation, human inter-rater agreement was approximately 98\% while 87\% of LLM answers exactly matched consensus, 2\% partially, and 9\% did not. Mean question-level accuracy was 91.5\% (SD 13.4\%) across 157 questions with at least 20 answers, and declined as ambiguity increased, from 96\% for Medication/Event Flag to 62\% for Event Timing questions. Conclusions: LLMs answering clinical registry questions on unprocessed EMR data achieved far lower accuracy than human abstractors. LLM accuracy fell steadily as ambiguity and the level of required clinical reasoning increased.

title: A benchmark of large language models for spatially informed proposal generation in local search for the p-median problem
abstract: The p -median problem is a classical, NP-hard model in location science, and decades of research have produced exact, heuristic, and meta-heuristic algorithms to solve it. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) have begun to assist in optimization by interpreting problem descriptions and generating solver code; however, their intrinsic ability to reason about spatial structure in facility-location problems remains underexplored. We introduce an LLM-as-proposer framework for the discrete p-median problem that embeds an LLM within a classical local search with external evaluation. The LLM's contribution as a spatially informed proposer is evaluated within a controlled search structure and compared fairly with established heuristics. We benchmark the proposed framework with three frontier LLMs on six TSPLIB point sets commonly used in location analysis across multiple p facilities, comparing against (i) exact mixed-integer problem references and (ii) five classical heuristics and meta-heuristics baselines. Across all settings, LLM-guided search consistently outperforms greedy baselines, frequently attains near-optimal solutions on small-to-medium instances, and evaluates orders of magnitude fewer objectives than tabu search, although inference remains the dominant runtime cost. Prompt ablation further shows that some spatial summaries materially improve robustness on larger instances, whereas some local diagnostic cues can be counterproductive. Taken together, these results show that contemporary LLMs exhibit meaningful spatial reasoning as proposers in p-Median local search, while also clarifying the current gap to mature meta-heuristics in solution quality and computational efficiency, motivating continued exploration of hybrid designs as LLMs become more capable.

title: Brownfield Tercihi: Beş İşlem, Bir Doktrin ve Türkiye'nin Geç Kalmış Sermaye Hesabı
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Vol.1 No.5, küresel madencilik sermayesinin 2024 sonundan 2026 ortasına kadar uzanan 18 aylık penceresinde beş bayrak işlem üzerinden gözlemlenen ortak refleksi inceliyor: brownfield (kahverengi saha) tercihi. BHP'nin Microsoft Azure üzerinde Escondida ve Spence sahalarında flotasyon devresine yerleştirdiği foundation model katmanı, mevcut cevherden ek tenör çıkartmanın yeni keşiften ucuz olduğunu kanıtlıyor — bu, algoritmik bir kira biçimidir ve Türkiye bakır sahalarına lisans bağımlılığı olarak yansıyacaktır. Glencore, Trafigura ve Mercuria'nın Merdeka için kurmaya çalıştığı satın alma konsorsiyumu, fiziksel tüccarın "alıcıdan sahibe" dönüşümünü işaret ediyor; bu, altın tedarik zincirinde yeni bir aracı sınıfının ve Türkiye için offtake müzakere asimetrisinin habercisi. Soma A'nın 436 milyon TL'lik devri, fiyatlanmamış kapatma yükümlülüğünün özelleştirme bedelini sembolik kıldığı bir vakadır; havzada gerçek değer kömürde değil, dekapaj sahası ve rehabilitasyon arsasının opsiyon değerindedir. Codelco-SQM'in 3 milyar dolarlık Atacama yapısı, devlet ortaklığını maliyet primi olarak değil veri-paylaşım rejimi olarak kurguluyor; Türkiye Eti Maden modeli için karşılaştırmalı bir muhasebe ödevidir. Antofagasta'nın Zaldívar'da 900 milyon dolar yatırarak primer sülfürü klorür liçle çözmesi, brownfield'ın kimyasal yeniden tasarımla nasıl ömür uzatıldığını gösteriyor — ve Çayeli, Murgul, Küre için yapılmamış soruyu masaya koyuyor. Beş vaka tek doktrini doğruluyor: sermaye yeni jeoloji aramıyor, mevcut jeolojiyi yeni kimya ve yeni veriyle yeniden okuyor. Türkiye'nin 2026-2028 penceresindeki base-case riski, brownfield ekonomisinin gerektirdiği teknik kapasiteyi kuramadan yeşil saha söylemine bağlı kalmasıdır.

title: ESAA-Conversational: An Event-Sourced Memory Layer for Continuity, Handoff, and Curation Across Heterogeneous LLM Coding Agents
abstract: Software developers increasingly work with multiple LLM coding agents, switching among tools such as Codex, Grok, Claude Code, and other assistants as context windows fill, sessions end, or a particular agent becomes better suited to a subtask. Each agent, however, persists its conversation in a private and vendor-specific log. The result is conversational state drift: goals, decisions, open tasks, and rationales established with one agent are not reliably available when another agent takes over. This paper presents \emph{ESAA-Conversational}, a domain specialization of Event-Sourcing Agent Architecture (ESAA)~\cite{esaa} for shared conversational memory across heterogeneous agents. The method treats the visible conversation as a local event store: hooks and watchers capture visible turns, normalize them into an append-only \texttt{activity.jsonl}, and deterministically project read models such as \texttt{handoff.md}, \texttt{state.md}, \texttt{decisions.md}, and \texttt{tasks.json}. Mechanical capture does not require LLM inference; agents use judgment only for explicit curation, recording durable decisions and conversational tasks through domain commands. The public v1.1.0 release implements a PowerShell CLI with \texttt{init}, \texttt{enable-hooks}, \texttt{sync}, \texttt{project}, \texttt{verify}, \texttt{context}, \texttt{decide}, and \texttt{task}; includes \texttt{workspace\_root} isolation and a write-path lockfile; and is distributed as a greenfield package with an empty public log. A self-referential case study with 570 development-lab events shows that heterogeneous agents can collaborate through a shared log without a direct agent-to-agent channel, while the public distribution preserves privacy by excluding the private conversational history.

title: Patent Analysis of Providing Services Related to Item Delivery via 3D Manufacturing on Demand: US9898776B2
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Purpose: To systematically examine the patent and evaluate its technological, strategic, and commercial significance in the emerging field of on-demand digital manufacturing. The study aims to investigate how the patented invention integrates customer ordering, additive manufacturing, and delivery management into a unified ecosystem that enhances customization, reduces inventory dependency, and improves supply-chain efficiency. Furthermore, the article seeks to assess the patent’s innovation potential, business value, societal impact, and future opportunities through structured analytical frameworks, thereby contributing to knowledge creation in the domains of 3D manufacturing, e-commerce, and technology-driven logistics. Methodology: This study adopts an exploratory qualitative research approach to systematically analyze the selected patent. Relevant data were collected from open-access sources, including Google Search, Google Patents, Google Scholar, and AI-powered GPT tools, and were subsequently organized and interpreted according to the study objectives. Structured analytical frameworks such as SWOC and ABCDEF were applied to generate meaningful insights into the patent's technological, strategic, and commercial significance. Results & Analysis: The analysis reveals that the patent “Providing Services Related to Item Delivery via 3D Manufacturing on Demand” introduces a transformative framework that integrates customer ordering, digital design management, distributed 3D manufacturing, and intelligent delivery services into a unified ecosystem. The results indicate significant advantages in terms of inventory reduction, mass customization, supply-chain optimization, localized production, and enhanced customer satisfaction, while also highlighting challenges related to intellectual property protection, cybersecurity, quality assurance, and infrastructure requirements. Overall, the study demonstrates that the patent possesses strong technological innovation, substantial commercial potential, and strategic relevance for the future development of Industry 4.0, smart manufacturing, and on-demand digital commerce systems. Originality & Values: The originality of this patent analysis lies in its unique integration of customer ordering, digital design management, on-demand 3D manufacturing, and intelligent delivery coordination within a single end-to-end ecosystem. The study adds scholarly value by demonstrating how digital inventories, distributed manufacturing networks, and mass customization can transform traditional production and supply-chain models into flexible, customer-centric systems. Furthermore, the patent offers significant technological, commercial, and societal value by supporting sustainable manufacturing, reducing inventory dependence, and enabling next-generation Industry 4.0 business models. title: Integrated Model to Improve the Order Fill Rate Using SLP, WMS and Generative AI in a Fast-Moving Consumer Goods Distribution Center
authors: Allison Dunia Siles Olivera; Mylena Ivonne Hipolito Osorio
source_name: Repositorio Académico UPC (Universidad Peruana de Ciencias Aplicadas)
abstract: El bajo cumplimiento de pedidos completos, medido mediante el indicador Order Fill Rate (OFR), representa una limitación crítica en la eficiencia de los procesos logísticos de distribución en empresas del sector consumo masivo. En respuesta a esta problemática, se plantea un modelo integrado que combina herramientas de mejora continua, como Systematic Layout Planning (SLP) con tecnologías emergentes como la inteligencia artificial generativa (GenAI) y un sistema WMS. El objetivo del modelo es estandarizar el proceso de gestión de pedidos, optimizar el layout del almacén y automatizar la verificación y consolidación de órdenes. La validación se realizó mediante simulación en el software Arena, considerando una operación anual de 340 días, 22 vendedores y más de 480 pedidos diarios. Se evaluaron variables como pedidos completos, errores de picking, tiempos de operación y reprocesos. El modelo propuesto incrementó el OFR de 90.86% a 98.00%, redujo a 0% los errores por registros incompletos y productos mal ubicados, y mejoró el tiempo de operación por pedido en un 16.57%. Desde una perspectiva financiera, el proyecto fue evaluado mediante flujos económicos y análisis de riesgo con @Risk, obteniendo un VANF de S/ 36,123.38, TIR de 24.09% y una RBCF de 1.16. Estos resultados demuestran que el modelo es viable, tanto técnica como económicamente, para mejorar la eficiencia operativa en centros de distribución.

title: Integrating AI-Agents into the Digital Transformation of Business Processes of Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises
authors: Volodymyr A. Kuchynskyi; Anton M. Kuzmynskyi
abstract: The article explores the theoretical and practical foundations of digitalizing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the context of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0) through the use of AI agents as a tool for the systematic transformation of business processes. Based on the DESI index and OECD data, it highlights the lag of domestic SMEs compared to Central European indicators of digital maturity and the need to shift from reactive automation to proactive, data-driven management. The article explains the essence of an AI agent as an autonomous system based on large language models (LLMs), capable of planning complex sequences of actions (chain-of-thought reasoning) and integrating with external APIs. Through a comparative analysis of traditional and agent-based AI, it is shown that, unlike narrowly specialized solutions, agent-based systems create a fundamentally new economic logic of automation. The results of an empirical study of 28 domestic SMEs show that 55% of companies are already using AI in marketing, 48% in customer support, but more complex operational tasks remain outside the scope of automation, confirming the mainly tactical nature of current AI implementation in the sector. The key areas of technology application were systematized, including: automating up to 80% of customer inquiries, predictive scoring in marketing, financial accounting in cloud environments (BAS, Xero), and supply chain optimization. A conceptual four-stage model for step-by-step implementation of AI agents in SMEs was proposed (from strategic diagnostics and piloting based on low-code platforms to achieving digital maturity over 18+ months). It was found that integrating autonomous systems allows SMEs to achieve the effect of «scaling without cost increase» and democratizes access to advanced analytics. Despite existing risks of technological dependence (vendor lock-in) and model «hallucinations», AI agents are becoming a strategic factor in boosting competitiveness and institutional learning for businesses in the Industry 4.0 era.

title: CRAYON: Hardware-Accelerated BPE Tokenization via Zero-Copy Double-Array Tries and SIMD Vectorization
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Subword tokenization is a critical preprocessing gate in Large Language Model (LLM) inference and training pipelines.Traditional tokenizers rely on pointer-heavy trie structures or dynamic hash tables, introducing severe memory fragmentation, highpointer-chasing latencies, and significant cold-start loading overheads. This paper presents CRAYON, a systems-first BPE tokenizationframework that represents vocabulary matching using memory-aligned Double-Array Tries (DAT). CRAYON achieves zero-copy,sub-millisecond vocabulary swaps via operating system memory mapping. To optimize inference, CRAYON integrates an optimistic AVX2SIMD scanning pathway that processes 32-byte ASCII blocks in a single instruction cycle, bypassing UTF-8 validation overhead whensafe. For massive parallel batch processing, CRAYON introduces a GPU-accelerated parallel lookup engine in CUDA and ROCm/HIP,bypassing thread-wide lock contention through dynamic batch capacity planning. Furthermore, CRAYON implements a mathematicallyexact greedy BPE training algorithm optimized via a parallel-array linked list, an inverted occurrence index, and a lazy max-heap priorityqueue. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that CRAYON achieves CPU throughput exceeding 18.4 million tokens/sec on standardbenchmarks, outperforming Rust-based implementations by up to 35×, while maintaining a cold-start initialization latency of only 0.54 ms.

title: Internal Credit and External Blame: Self-Attribution in Operations and Supply Chain Performance
authors: Yimeng Niu; Xiao Qiao; Jing Wu; Xingsheng Yang
abstract: Problem definition: This study examines self-attribution tendencies and their associated outcomes in operations management (OM) performance evaluation, in which managers are not always objective when giving credit to outcomes. They may attribute strong performance to internal factors (“internal credit”) while assigning poor performance to external factors (“external blame”). Methodology: Large language models based on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct are fine-tuned to analyze earnings call Q&A transcripts and construct a firm-level measure of OM self-attribution. The superiority of LLM's performance is validated against traditional NLP approaches (Gradient Boosting, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Random Forest) and alternative LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o). The LLM-based measures are then used in Multinomial Logit models and fixed-effect models to assess the existence of self-attribution and its associations with subsequent outcomes. Results: Empirical analysis reveals a consistent pattern of OM self-attribution: managers claim internal credit for intra-organizational actions while assigning external blame to supply chain partners or macroeconomic conditions. This pattern persists after controlling for managers' experiences, Q&A sequencing, leading questions, contextual factors, and uncertainty in LLM outputs. OM self-attribution is more prevalent among larger firms, firms led by more experienced managers, and firms with lower operational efficiency and supply chain risk. Whereas non-OM financial self-attribution has been documented as a psychological bias, OM self-attribution exhibits a distinctive diplomatic and constructive nature. In contrast to the temporary effect of non-OM financial self-attribution, OM self-attribution is associated with real changes to financial and operational outcomes. Firms with stronger OM self-attribution tendencies receive more positive market and media responses and tend to have better future positioning in production and demand management and supply chain optimization. Theoretical and Managerial Implications: This study complements existing work on financial self-attribution by identifying a unique pattern of self-attribution in the OM context that functions as a strategic illusion of managerial control. OM self-attribution can be interpreted as a strategy where managers strategically shape attributions to signal active engagement in an uncertain environment, ultimately associated with positive future firm performance.

title: Supplementary Material for: Integrating Psychosocial Factors into Artificial Intelligence Models for Predicting Addiction Treatment Outcomes: A Systematic Review
authors: figshare admin karger; Martínez-Montás G.F.; Iniesta-Sepúlveda M.; Colón-Santana O.
abstract: Introduction: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into addiction research has expanded rapidly, yet it remains unclear how psychosocial, behavioral, and social-structural determinants are incorporated into predictive models of addiction treatment outcomes. Because recovery is strongly shaped by psychological, social, and environmental context, assessing how AI approaches operationalize these dimensions is essential for developing clinically meaningful and equitable tools. Methods: We conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed studies published from January 1, 2020 to October 30, 2025 across PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Eligible studies applied artificial intelligence or machine learning (ML) models to addiction treatment outcomes and explicitly included psychosocial, behavioral, or social-structural predictors. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and evaluated methodological quality using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB-2) domain structures. The protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) and in PROSPERO. Results: Fifteen studies met inclusion criteria, including electronic health record (EHR), administrative-, claims-based, program-level clinical models and psychosocial assessment datasets, digital phenotyping/ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies, natural language processing/large language model (NLP/LLM) approaches, and one causal ML analysis of randomized controlled trial data. Across modalities, models consistently identified housing instability, psychiatric comorbidity, employment status, craving, stress, legal involvement, prior overdose, treatment history, medication adherence, and neighborhood disadvantage as influential predictors of treatment dropout, discontinuation, overdose risk, relapse, or poor engagement—often adding prognostic value beyond medication-related, diagnostic, and routinely available clinical variables. EMA and digital phenotyping showed the highest short-term predictive accuracy for near-term risk prediction, whereas structured EHR-, administrative-, claims-based, and program-level clinical models achieved moderate but clinically actionable performance. Methodological quality was moderate overall, with limited external validation and infrequent assessment of calibration, fairness, transportability, or reproducibility practices. Conclusion: Current evidence indicates that psychosocial, behavioral, and social-structural determinants are central to AI-based prediction of addiction treatment outcomes. Although findings are promising, existing models remain preliminary and should not yet guide clinical decisions without external validation and implementation evaluation. Future work should prioritize multi-site validation, transparent reporting, fairness evaluation, and co-development with clinicians and individuals with lived experience to ensure that AI tools strengthen person-centered and equitable addiction care.

title: Advancing Pediatric Radiology Through Artificial Intelligence: Global Progress and Implications for Middle- and Low-Income Countries
authors: Sana Amreen; Ahmed Khairy; Fakeha Masood; Ngan Chu; Anju Paudel; Abdelrahman Aly Mohamed; Ayantoyinbo Oluwabusayomi; Yossef S. Alnasser
abstract: Background: Radiology underpins diagnosis and treatment across pediatrics, yet most artificial intelligence (AI) tools are developed for adults and validated on adult datasets only. Of more than 200 AI systems cleared by the United States (U.S.) Food and Drug Administration (FDA), only about 3% include pediatric validation. Because children differ from adults in anatomy, physiology, pathology, epidemiology, and imaging protocols, adult-trained models often perform sub-optimally in pediatric settings. Methods: A narrative review of peer-reviewed literature from 2000 to 2025 was conducted using PubMed, MEDLINE, Google Scholar, and Scopus. Studies involving AI applications in pediatric X-ray, ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), echocardiography, and point-of-care ultrasound with quantitative performance metrics were included. Findings were synthesized by imaging modality, clinical task, and differences between high-income countries (HICs) and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Results: AI demonstrated strong performance across multiple pediatric imaging tasks. In X-ray interpretation, AI detected fractures with area under the curve (AUC) values up to 0.96 (sensitivity, 90.8%; specificity, 88.7%). Pneumonia classification achieved 76.5% accuracy, and foreign body aspiration detection showed 95.3% specificity in HICs. In ultrasound, AI improved junior sonographers’ detection of intussusception (AUC 0.857 to 0.966) and reduced scan time by more than 50%. AI-assisted bone age estimation achieved a mean error of 0.39 years. In echocardiography, AI-derived ejection fraction showed excellent agreement with experts’ interclass correlation coefficient (ICC 0.983), and AI support improved atrioventricular septal defect detection (84.4% to 86.5%). In MRI, the use of AI enhanced lesion detection and supported quantitative analysis. Deep-learning models trained on routine T1- and T2-weighted sequences predicted liver stiffness across multi-site datasets, while advanced neuroimaging pipelines improved the identification of subtle epileptogenic lesions that are often missed on conventional pediatric MRI. However, adult-trained models showed limited generalizability to children. Still, excluding children under the age of two years improved the reading accuracy of pediatric chest X-rays (CXRs) by adult-trained models from 88% to 97%. AI faces challenges beyond the development of age-specific models. Substantial heterogeneity, limited pediatric-specific datasets, and unresolved medicolegal responsibility further restrict adoption worldwide. Challenges are amplified in LMICs, where unstable electricity, limited radiology resources, weak digital infrastructure, and scarce pediatric providers limit implementation. Additionally, many large language models underperform and lack inclusive algorithms suitable for pediatric radiology in many LMICs. Conclusions: AI can enhance diagnostic accuracy, efficiency, and access to pediatric imaging, particularly in resource-limited settings, through task-shifting and decision support. However, it cannot replace pediatric radiologists as of today. Safe adoption requires pediatric-specific model development, standardized validation metrics, diverse datasets that include LMIC populations, stronger digital infrastructure, robust radiologist training in AI capabilities, and the establishment of clear guidelines and medicolegal policies.

title: AI in Management and Business Research
authors: Łukasz Sułkowski; Marcin Lis; Zdzisława Dacko-Pikiewicz; Katarzyna Szczepańska‐Woszczyna
abstract: Authors examine the transformative impact of artificial intelligence across key managerial domains, including predictive decision support, process automation, supply chain optimization, personalized customer experiences, human resources analytics, and global market intelligence. Rather than treating AI as a neutral tool, we situate it within organizational theory, conceptualizing it as a collaborative agent embedded in routines, highlighting principles of human–AI teaming, accountable algorithms, and the coproduction of decisions. This perspective underscores the need for frameworks that align analytics initiatives with strategic objectives, organizational values, and ethical standards. The chapter also provides practical guidance for implementing AI responsibly in managerial contexts. It addresses bias and fairness audits, particularly in sensitive applications like hiring and performance evaluation, emphasizes transparency to sustain stakeholder trust, and considers organizational change management and workforce reskilling to adapt to AI-augmented workflows. Illustrative vignettes demonstrate how explainable models facilitate managerial sensemaking, enabling leaders to interpret insights while maintaining decision authority. Additionally, generative AI is shown to accelerate product development and communication design when integrated under human oversight, balancing speed and creativity with contextual judgment. Overall, the chapter presents an integrated view of AI as a strategic, collaborative, and ethically grounded force within contemporary management practice.

title: Toward Self-Evolution-Ready Workflow Harnesses: A Reversible Migration Path and Convertibility Taxonomy for Expert LLM Pipelines
authors: Yimo Lin; Zhen Zhang; Yibin Li
abstract: While expert-validated "LLM + script" workflows deliver significant value, they remain static: they encode hard-won domain knowledge yet fail to adapt execution based on feedback. Existing agent research predominantly targets greenfield agents and synthetic benchmarks, leaving the migration of active legacy workflows unresolved. To bridge this gap, we present a reversible, Strangler-Fig migration path that refactors legacy workflows into composable, typed, and auditable stages. Central to this framework is a three-tier convertibility taxonomy (A/B/C), implemented as a routing stage within the system harness, which diagnoses a workflow's readiness and routes it accordingly.
