ScRNAseq and flow cytometry identified a unique expanded B cell population in tumor draining lymph nodes (tdLN) treated with T-VEC and anti-PD1 treatment. This study investigates the functional role of these B cells in our model. Methods: Mice grafted with B16-OVA were pretreated with anti-PD1 for 14 days. Resistant tumors were treated with continued anti-PD1, T-VEC+anti-PD1, or anti-CD20 + T-VEC+anti-PD1. Tumor growth was monitored, and flow cytometry was used to phenotype immune response in the tumor and tdLNs. Results: B cell depletion (anti-CD20) enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of T-VEC in anti-PD1-resistant tumors, significantly prolonging median overall survival (OS) (anti-CD20 + T-VEC+anti-PD1: no median reached; T-VEC+anti-PD1: 39.5 days; anti-PD1 alone: 21 days) (Figure 1). Pooled experiments showed 6\/9 complete responses in the anti-CD20 + T-VEC + anti-PD1 group vs 3\/10 in the T-VEC + anti-PD1 group. Flow cytometry on day 7 confirmed efficient B cell depletion and enhanced effector T cell activity in tdLN, including increased granzyme B expression. Intratumorally, B cell depletion decreased total T cell proportions, including T regulatory cells. Conclusion: Our findings highlight a significant therapeutic improvement with B cell depletion in combination with T-VEC in anti-PD-1 resistant melanoma. These results suggest a pivotal role for B cells in modulating the immune response, and ongoing studies are focused on uncovering the precise populations and mechanisms driving this enhanced efficacy and its potential to reshape long-term immunity.Figure 1ChatGPT\u2019s Performance in Breast Cancer Imaging and Management: Are We There Yet? Luis A Hern\u00e1ndez-Flores, MD, Nicolai Gonz\u00e1lez Stoylov, MD, Yennifer Gardu\u00f1o, MD, Alejandra Garc\u00eda Gonz\u00e1lez, MD, Raymundo Mu\u00f1oz, MD, Roberta Padilla, MD, Sergio Contreras, MD, Ruben Cortes Gonzalez, MD, FACS Instituto Nacional de Ciencias M\u00e9dicas y Nutrici\u00f3n Salvador Zubir\u00e1n, Mexico City, Mexico; Universidad Austral de Chile, El Paso, TX; La Salle University, Mexico City, Mexico Introduction: Artificial intelligence continues to be increasingly integrated into clinical practices, yet its reliability in breast cancer (BC) diagnosis and management remains uncertain. This study evaluates ChatGPT\u2019s ability to interpret mammographic findings and assist in BC treatment compared with radiologists and oncologists. Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 63 patients with BC, of whom 45 patients (57 \u00b1 10 years) underwent mammography and had biopsy-confirmed BC. Imaging characteristics, including breast density, Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) classification, mass shape, margins, microcalcifications and malignancy risk, were assessed. Cohen\u2019s kappa (\u03ba) test was used to evaluate agreement between ChatGPT and multidisciplinary teams for imaging interpretation and treatment decisions. Results: Of 45 patients, 93.3% showed a clear mass. Most cases were categorized as BI-RADS 5 (73%) or 4 (27%), with irregular shape (65.1%) and spiculated margins (79.1%). ChatGPT showed perfect agreement (\u03ba = 1.000 p \u2264 0.001) in identifying high-risk lesions (BI-RADS \u22654) and fair agreement for mass detection (\u03ba = 0.365, p = 0.013), but poor agreement in distinguishing between BI-RADS classification (\u03ba = 0.097), mass margins (\u03ba = 0.038), and microcalcification (\u03ba = -0.055). For BC management, chemotherapy\/hormonal therapy recommendations showed moderate agreement (\u03ba = 0.516, p = 0.001). However, surgical and radiotherapy recommendations were unreliable (Figure 1). Conclusion: ChatGPT successfully identified high-risk lesions but failed in detailed BI-RADS classification and surgical treatment decisions. Its unreliable performance in surgical and radiotherapy recommendations underscores the limitations of current AI models in BC diagnosis and management. Further refinement is necessary before clinical implementation.Figure 1Clinical Characteristics and Racial Disparity in Acral Lentiginous Melanoma with In-Transit Metastases Shanie Shemla, MD, Andreina Giron, MD, Xavier De Pena-Pena, MD, Charlotte E Ariyan, MD, FACS, Edmund K Bartlett, MD, FACS, Mary S Brady, MD, FACS, Danielle M Bello, MD, FACS Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY; Children\u2019s Hospital of Orange County, Orange, CA Introduction: Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) is a rare subtype, disproportionately impacting Black and Hispanic populations and is associated with worse outcomes compared with cutaneous melanoma. In-transit metastases (ITM) occur between the primary tumor and nearest lymph node basin and can develop with any melanoma subtype. While some aspects of ALM have been studied, data regarding ITM in ALM remains scarce. We present long-term follow-up of ALM with ITM, providing clinicopathologic features of this rare disease. Methods: Retrospective cohort of 90 ALM patients with ITM treated at a single institution (2001-2021) with >6 months follow-up. Demographic and clinical data were collected and analyzed using descriptive statistics. Results: Median follow-up was approximately 5 years and median time from diagnosis to ITM recurrence was 14 months. Disease-specific mortality was 52% (vs 45% in our entire ITM cohort), 22% remained without evidence of disease and median overall survival was 52 months. Patient characteristics are presented in Table 1. Among 11 Black patients, 73% died of disease vs 49% of 71 White patients. Late stage (III\/IV) at diagnosis was seen in 64% of Black patients vs 53% of White patients. Additionally, 45% of Black patients had nodal\/distant disease at time of recurrence vs 34% of White patients. Conclusion: ITM in ALM is associated with poor outcomes, consistent with prior studies. Our findings highlight racial disparity, with Black patients experiencing a higher rate of disease-related mortality. Late diagnosis and more extensive disease can partially account for this difference, emphasizing the need for early detection and equitable access to care. title: Leveraging Large Language Models for Risk Assessment in Hyperconnected Logistic Hub Network Deployment
authors: Yinzhu Quan; Yujia Xu; Guanlin Chen; Benoît Montreuil; IMT Mines Albi; Frédérick Bénaben
abstract: The growing emphasis on energy efficiency and environmental sustainability in global supply chains introduces new challenges in the deployment of hyperconnected logistics hubs. In such volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) logistics networks, risk assessment becomes essential to ensure successful hub deployment. However, traditional methods often struggle to effectively capture and analyze unstructured textual information. In this paper, we leverage large language models (LLMs) with tools to conduct risk assessment for logistics hub deployment. We use LLMs to identify potential risks by analyzing unstructured data, such as geopolitical factors, regulatory changes, and environmental risks. These data are integrated into tools, which can be automatically called by the LLMs to support our decision-making process. In addition, we design prompts to instruct LLMs to assess the feasibility of hub selection by analyzing risk types and levels, and then providing insights for hub location recommendations. Finally, we conduct a comparative analysis of new and existing hub locations to evaluate improvements in risk mitigation and overall network resilience.

title: Optimizing Retail with AI: How Intelligent Systems Are Redefining Shopping Experiences

abstract: The retail industry is undergoing a fundamental transformation driven by artificial intelligence technologies that are redefining how businesses operate and engage with customers. This comprehensive review explores the multifaceted impact of AI across the retail value chain, from personalized recommendation systems to predictive inventory management. The integration of sophisticated machine learning algorithms enables retailers to process vast amounts of customer data, creating hyperpersonalized experiences that adapt to individual preferences in real-time. Deep learning architectures, particularly neural collaborative filtering and transformer-based models, have revolutionized recommendation systems, while generative AI technologies are transforming demand forecasting and supply chain optimization. Beyond these core applications, AI permeates every aspect of retail operations, including dynamic pricing, computer vision analytics, chatbot-powered customer service, and warehouse automation. However, successful AI implementation faces significant challenges, including data quality issues, organizational resistance, ethical considerations, and substantial financial investments. The evidence suggests that achieving meaningful returns from AI requires not just technological sophistication but comprehensive organizational learning capabilities, strategic vision, and robust governance frameworks. As the retail landscape continues to evolve, AI emerges not merely as a competitive advantage but as an essential foundation for sustainable success in an increasingly digital marketplace.

title: Exploring the world for longitudinal datasets: data resources for transformative mental health research
authors: Louise Arseneault; Bridget T. Bryan; Thomas Canning; Malaika Okundi; Alice Stephens; Elena Triantafillopoulou; Daniel Yu; Mariana Bolivar; Parisa Mansoori; Lea Milligan; Ed Evans; Grace Gatera
abstract: Key to our understanding of mental health conditions are longitudinal data that allow the examination of developmental patterns and factors that precipitate, increase, buffer or parallel mental ill health. A priority is to maximize the use of the data already collected by existing studies, given their research and financial value. A global effort to seek out longitudinal datasets worldwide could serve as a catalyst for boosting the uptake of data and maximizing the value for money of existing data resources. For more than half of the population worldwide, the onset of mental health conditions typically occurs before the age of 25 [1–3]. Longitudinal studies that start in the early years of life, prior to the typical onset of mental health conditions, allow for a deeper understanding of temporal trends and causal mechanisms that can explain how environmental, biological, and genetic factors influence mental health conditions. In addition to the data they collect, longitudinal studies are instrumental because of the populations they represent. Groups of individuals at increased risk for mental health conditions are especially valuable for developmental research. Sample size is another consideration; larger groups of individuals enable the exploration of important factors with smaller effect sizes and mitigate the impact of participant attrition across time. Additionally, the granularity of assessment enhances the worth of longitudinal studies by capturing rapid changes during pivotal life stages and transitions. This is especially pertinent in childhood, a foundational period for learning and experimentation, and during adolescence, characterized by sudden physical changes and expanding social networks. We undertook a global search for existing longitudinal datasets to provide a springboard for innovative mental health research by leveraging the current landscape of longitudinal data resources. We report here an overview of the datasets we identified, their overall richness and areas for enrichment, and observations to consider as we expand longitudinal data resources. Figure 1 represents our process for identifying all longitudinal datasets from across the world, including those that delved into mental health and other research topics including physical health or socioeconomic factors. We examined datasets without mental health data to date, as well as those rich in mental health data. We considered datasets to be longitudinal if they spanned a minimum of two waves of data collection. We surveyed cohorts (which follow a group of individuals over time) and household/community panels (which use the household or the community as the unit of analysis over time). We also inspected data collected routinely for non-research purposes (e.g. health registries, surveillance panels) and biobanks (i.e. repositories of human biological samples) with multiple waves of data collection. We included datasets in any language. We excluded cross-sectional studies and randomized controlled trials. Flowchart presenting the key partners and the stages for landscaping longitudinal datasets worldwide. For datasets in academia, we adopted an active search approach for identifying longitudinal datasets which involved looking through repositories containing information about multiple datasets, such as academic journals and global consortia. Examples of repositories include the Maelstrom Research platform, the International Network for the Demographic Evaluation of Populations and Their Health (INDEPTH) Data Repository, and the Health Data Research Gateway. We screened academic journals such as the International Journal of Epidemiology and Advances in Life Course Research for cohort profile papers. We also pulled datasets from global constoria, such as the International Household Survey Network, the Asia Pacific Cohort Studies Collaboration, and the International Hundred Thousand Cohorts Consortium. We also adopted a passive search approach which involved receiving information from individuals across the world in the mental health and epidemiology communities regarding datasets and repositories. For datasets outside academia, the team engaged in three complementary approaches. First, approaching industry contacts to identify relevant datasets and discuss barriers to sharing non-academic data. Second, searching open data portals using an automated strategy. Third, using desk research to focus on the most promising types of non-academic datasets previously identified. We explored all identified longitudinal datasets to unravel the richness of their data and their populations. This scoping exercise was guided by our experience reviewing thousands of longitudinal datasets and by the input from stakeholders who took part in a Theory of Change (ToC) process. ToC processes are used to define the steps that need to happen for a desired outcome to be achieved [4–6]. For this project, the ToC process informed how longitudinal datasets could be enriched to facilitate transformative mental health research. We adopted a co-production methodology by involving individuals with lived experience (LE) of mental health conditions, as well as researchers and policymakers from various countries and demographic backgrounds. Their input was captured through a pre-workshop package, an online workshop discussion, and a post-workshop meeting. The ToC process occurred alongside the search, allowing the findings and insights from each process to inform the other [7]. We screened longitudinal datasets according to benchmark criteria proposed by the Wellcome Trust. The benchmarks were that a longitudinal dataset: Consists of at least 8000 participants at inception; Has collected, or has the potential to collect, data from participants at some point between the ages of 14 and 30; Has collected data at least every 3 years, or can contact participants to invite them for more frequent data collection; Has collected data in the last 3 years, has plans to collect new data, or is in contact with participants. From the 6747 unique datasets we screened, we identified over 3000 longitudinal datasets from around the world (Fig. 2). The large number of datasets that we identified during our comprehensive investigation include data collected from over 700 million individuals in 146 countries. A total of 100 longitudinal initiatives were ongoing, based on large samples, and had granular assessments of young populations. Most datasets enrolled fewer than 8000 participants at their inception (Fig. 3). However, a subset stands out with exceptionally large sample sizes. These large data sources are often based on routinely collected data from health and government records, or multi-site initiatives. Our scoping exercise underscores the wealth and range of existing longitudinal data for exploring developmental patterns of mental health conditions. Flowchart reporting the number of datasets processed during the landscaping stages. Number of participants at inception for all identified longitudinal datasets. Our investigation revealed an unequal distribution of longitudinal datasets worldwide. A considerable proportion of the identified datasets originated from Europe (40%). This region encompasses 44 primarily affluent countries, distinguishing it from other regions with a greater number of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). For instance, Africa, the Middle East, and Asia include 104 countries that are primarily LMICs and generated 25% of the overall identified longitudinal resources. In contrast, the Americas, which encompass 36 countries and represent some LMICs, contributed an equivalent of 25% of the total identified longitudinal datasets. We noted a few longitudinal resources in LMICs, which disproportionately face economic and geopolitical challenges. The concentration of study populations and research infrastructure in wealthy Western countries limits the generalizability of mental health research findings [8, 9]. Mental health has rarely taken precedence for large longitudinal initiatives, and those with a specific focus on mental health tend to be smaller in scale (Fig. 4). More than 75% of the datasets that focus on mental health have enrolled fewer than 5000 participants. Several factors may contribute to this pattern. Firstly, mental health may not have been a priority for policy and funding when the studies were established [10, 11], leading to a scarcity of resources dedicated to expansive mental health-focused longitudinal studies. Secondly, the limited evidence-based avenues for transformative mental health interventions result in pathways for action that are less clear than for physical health conditions. This may hinder the motivation for large-scale mental health research. Thirdly, the challenges associated with the assessment of mental health conditions could contribute to the preference for smaller size and more targeted studies. Collectively, these considerations underscore the need for increased focus, resources, and innovative approaches to enhance the integration of mental health assessments within larger-scale longitudinal datasets. We clustered them into four categories representing domains within the broader landscape of mental health research. This categorization offers a structured framework for researchers and funders to navigate and explore the specific areas where these datasets can contribute. Richness in mental health measures: strong measurement of depression and anxiety, valuable resources for psychosis research, consideration of other mental health conditions, and mental health across the life course. Value in targeted populations: high-risk groups, under-represented groups, populations from under-represented locations, ageing populations, and value in the long run. Diversity of data: factors contributing to mental health conditions, neuroimaging data, wearables and phone apps, biological and genetic data, and routinely collected data. Mental health embedded in wider context: mental health within social context, the impact of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, connectivity between datasets, natural disasters and geopolitical factors, and interventions embedded in longitudinal datasets. The global distribution of longitudinal datasets across various categories of richness showcases contributions from all geographical regions: Africa, the Middle East, and Asia (7% of total longitudinal datasets from this region), the Americas (15%), Europe and the Pacific (12%), and cross-regions (8%). The representation of minoritized and marginalized groups was insufficient or absent in most longitudinal datasets. Individuals, such as those from ethnically or racially minoritized groups [12], Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) communities [13], neurodivergent individuals [14, 15], and people experiencing homelessness [16] are at a elevated risk of mental ill health and more likely to be missed during recruitment or lost to follow-up in longitudinal research. As a result, these groups are often under-represented in longitudinal research unless explicitly targeted. Recruitment in longitudinal research ought to be set out with a commitment to maintaining diverse and representative samples, recognizing that inclusive datasets are fundamental for generating findings that resonate with the broader population. This approach not only safeguards against biases for interpreting mental health trends but also fosters an equitable understanding of the factors influencing mental health outcomes across diverse groups. Our review highlighted variation in methods and instruments employed to measure mental health conditions, including standardized and tailor-made measures. There are many ways to assess mental health conditions as they are contingent upon various considerations such as the unique characteristics of the population when selecting instruments. It is important that researchers opt for measures that are most appropriate for participants’ developmental stage and are cognizant of contextual nuances including cultural features. Copyright and language translation requirements can also prevent the use of shared measures across borders and different languages. There is no one-size-fits-all approach to assessing mental health conditions and variation in measurement offers the flexibility required to appropriately assess mental health across diverse contexts and populations. However, this variation in measurement approaches has also, in part, arisen due to mental health often being treated as an afterthought. Most datasets identified in our search did not focus on mental health, such that the lack of a unified and standardized approach to measuring mental health may have led to difficulties in selecting high-quality, widely used measures of mental health. The diversity in measures used in existing datasets poses challenges in comparing and synthesizing findings across studies and limits the generalizability and robustness of mental health research outcomes. Our review indicates a lack of longitudinal datasets that have incorporated involvement from LE experts (LEEs), communities, and healthcare service users when developing their program of research. The active involvement of the community and collaboration with LEEs contribute significantly to ensuring that longitudinal research is relevant to those who experience mental health conditions [17, 18]. This engagement enhances the applicability of research findings and supports the development of clinical practices that are sensitive to the real-world needs and experiences of individuals dealing with mental health challenges. While there is an increasing recognition of the importance of such involvement and engagement, their absence remains common in longitudinal research [19–21]. Expanding the involvement of LEEs, communities, and service users to longitudinal frameworks can contribute to more holistic, patient-centred, and culturally sensitive approaches to mental health research and intervention strategies [22]. Some recommendations emerged from our search, and they might provide useful insight as the field moves forward. A prudent consideration as we reflect on the richness of longitudinal datasets is the importance of studies that avoid covering every aspect of human development to optimize the value of a single dataset. The benefits of collecting a wealth of data from one sample should be weighed against significant drawbacks. Overburdening participants by collecting excessive data at frequent intervals may negatively affect participation rates and data quality over time. Instead of pursuing an exhaustive approach with individual studies, researchers and funders might explore the benefits of optimizing the value of groups of particularly promising studies. This can be achieved through concerted efforts in, for example, maximizing sample size, sharing measurement tools, or expanding the geographical location of participants. The collaborative development of consortia for longitudinal initiatives offers important advantages. These initiatives can work together, pooling expertise and data resources when synergies arise and proving especially beneficial for mental health research. Furthermore, recognizing the potential benefits of longitudinal research in diverse settings and cultures, it becomes imperative to foster cross-national initiatives that support the development and maintenance of longitudinal resources in LMICs. These initiatives can provide vital assistance to researchers in these nations navigating the complexities of collecting and sustaining data. By fostering collaboration and sharing expertise, these cross-national efforts contribute to a more inclusive and comprehensive understanding of temporal trends and patterns across diverse global contexts. This collaborative approach acknowledges the potential richness of data that may emerge from regions facing unique challenges and underscores the importance of global cooperation in advancing longitudinal research. Of utmost importance is ensuring that international collaboration is encouraged by funding schemes while leadership is shared equitably with the teams on site. There are clear benefits to capitalizing on the richness of existing datasets rather than investing in the creation of new longitudinal initiatives. Encouraging researchers to build upon the strengths of established datasets is a strategic approach that can foster collaboration across datasets to maximize the potential for mental health research. We did not find one single ideal source of data for comprehensive mental health research. By enriching groups of existing datasets that complement each other, researchers and funders can increase the value of data already collected by joining forces. This collaborative approach optimizes the efficiency of data collection and utilization, and fosters a more comprehensive understanding of mental health across diverse contexts and using different methods. There is a compelling need for the mental health research community to prioritize the consolidation and refinement of measurement tools to allow international comparisons across samples and cultures. This involves not only considering the diverse needs of different populations and contexts, but also establishing common standards and frameworks to enhance the consistency and comparability of mental health assessments. Decisions about how to assess mental health conditions should be rooted in careful methodological work that rigorously tests the adequacy of instruments. The complexity of existing measures poses challenges in reconciling findings, harmonizing data, and establishing international collaborations. Furthermore, investing in methodological work is imperative to verify whether measures collected during a different era are suitably comparable. This commitment to methodological rigour will enhance the quality and reliability of mental health research and contribute to the development of more standardized and comparable measurement tools for the future. The scarcity of emphasis on mental health within large-scale longitudinal initiatives may reflect a notable gap in research priorities and highlight the need for more concerted efforts to incorporate mental health considerations into the fabric of extensive and comprehensive longitudinal studies. The limited representation of mental health-focused datasets emphasizes the urgency of considering mental health within the broader context of longitudinal research given its profound contribution to individual and public health outcomes. Our search indicates an increasing emphasis on mental health, which we hope will continue. By carefully considering and optimizing data management and access, researchers and funders can enhance the uptake and overall impact and innovation of longitudinal data. A strategic approach would ensure that data are not only made available to a wide pool of researchers but are also easily accessible and effectively utilized for advancing transformative research in the field of mental health. title: REDEFINING RETAIL: THE TRANSFORMATIVE IMPACT OF AI ON THE RETAIL INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
authors: Carmel Karaniya Wigayha; Kenny Ryans Alexia
source_name: LOGIS (Logistics, Operations and Global Integration Studies)
abstract: The retail industry is undergoing a profound transformation driven by the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). This systematic review examines the impact of AI across key areas, including supply chain optimization, personalization, omnichannel strategies, and decision-making. Using data from peer-reviewed studies and visual analyses with VOSviewer, the review identifies major trends, such as the integration of predictive analytics, generative AI, and sustainability practices. It also highlights challenges, including algorithmic bias and data privacy concerns, while proposing strategies for ethical and inclusive AI adoption. The findings underscore the importance of interdisciplinary approaches and collaboration among stakeholders to harness AI’s potential for innovation and sustainable growth. This study contributes to both theoretical knowledge and practical applications, offering actionable insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers in the retail sector.

title: The 2024 Vizient Connections Summit Report
abstract: Reflect, Adapt, Evolve: A Report on the 2024 Vizient Connections Summit Rand Ballard, MS1, Simrit Sandhu, MBA, MS2, Julie Cerese, PhD, RN, MSN3, John Grande, MBA4, Juli Hermanson, MPH, RDN, CPHQ5 1Chief Customer Officer, Vizient 2President, Spend Management, Vizient 3Senior Vice President, Performance Management and National Networks, Vizient 4Senior Vice President/General Manager, Spend Management Services and Delivery, Vizient 5Senior Director, Member Education, VizientVizient is honored to share the incredible work presented at the 2024 Vizient Connections Summit in Las Vegas. As the convener of this gathering, Vizient aims to disseminate best practices and lessons learned throughout the health care industry, leading to nationwide improvements in cost, quality and access to care. Held annually, the summit occupies a unique place in the industry, bringing together a variety of stakeholders to address the most pressing challenges facing the U.S. health care system. The meeting serves as an interactive forum for a fragmented industry to come together as a single community across geographies and sectors. The 2024 Vizient Connections Summit attracted nearly 5000 attendees, including Vizient providers, suppliers, and partners. Held September 16-19 in Las Vegas, NV, the meeting emphasized the importance of reflection—the act of contemplating and learning from past experiences, accomplishments and failures as a foundation for growth and development. Reflection fosters continuous improvement and a deeper understanding of ourselves as individuals and of the world around us. It helps organizational leaders adapt in real-time to the present by clarifying current goals and evolve towards the future by charting a refined or new course that leverages emerging opportunities. It allows providers and caregivers to reaffirm their compassion and commitment to making a difference by rediscovering the true essence of their calling to heal, support and connect with individual patients. As Byron Jobe, president and chief executive officer (CEO) of Vizient, noted in his welcoming remarks at the summit, one of the most critical lessons of any reflective exercise is the importance of coming together to care for those in need. Anthropologists define advanced societies as those where communities work together. When examining human remains, they identify these communities by finding evidence of a femur bone that had healed from a previous break. In most prehistoric societies, a broken femur was a death sentence, as survival was impossible without assistance. As societies advanced, however, individuals with a broken femur no longer had to heal on their own. Communities came together to protect and heal the injured and vulnerable. Thus, the provision of health care is seen as a building block of advanced societies and thriving communities. “It comes back to the notion of a community coming together to care for those in need. That’s why we do what we do, that’s why we’re here together, and that’s why we celebrate.” —Byron Jobe, President and Chief Executive Officer, Vizient The importance of reflection became clear in the summit opening keynote address, delivered by Fritz Francois, MD, executive vice president, vice dean and chief of hospital operations at NYU Langone Health. In October 2012, NYU Langone faced the aftermath of Superstorm Sandy, which cut the main hospital’s power and flooded its floors. Everyone pulled together to evacuate patients in exceedingly difficult circumstances and took necessary steps to ensure safety. Initially told that it might be 1 or 2 years for the hospital to reopen fully, the leadership team embarked on a meticulous planning process that, combined with flawless execution by determined staff and partners, enabled NYU Langone to perform its first surgery less than 2 months later. Beyond managing the immediate crisis, NYU Langone’s leaders used the crisis as an opportunity to reimagine the organization and make it better for the long term. They began a process to redefine how work is done and worked to instill and draw from a culture of exceptionalism and a commitment to the principles of high-reliability organizations. These principles include (1) preoccupation with failure; (2) reluctance to simplify; (3) sensitivity to the local environment; (4) commitment to resilience; and (5) deference to expertise rather than authority and hierarchy. The result has been amazing, with NYU Langone consistently delivering high quality, cost-effective patient care across its system. Not surprisingly, NYU Langone has consistently ranked at the top of the Vizient Quality & Accountability (Q&A) performance scorecard. (More information on the Q&A scorecard appears in the next section.) “Understanding is attained only when acquisition is accompanied by constant reflection.” —American philosopher John Dewey, as quoted by Fritz Francois, MD, Executive Vice President, Vice Dean and Chief of Hospital Operations, NYU Langone Health, during his keynote address The meeting gave attendees much to reflect upon, with 185 educational sessions, including peer-to-peer meetings, presentations, panels, poster sessions and knowledge forums. The material represented the “best of the best” from Vizient providers, who collectively submitted nearly 800 abstracts (a new record, up from 647 in 2023). title: Decentralized Federated Learning Framework Privacy Preserving and Transport Supply Chain Optimization with Blockchain Anchoring
abstract: This paper creates a decentralised learning system that combines Federated Learning (FL) with blockchain based provenance to allow the stakeholders in the supply chain to weight predictive models without revealing raw data and keeping privacy intact, but increasing transparency. The study asserts long standing issues of data sensitivity, competitive confidentiality, and low inter organisational trust, which generally inhibit collaborative analytics in practicum supply chains setting. The conceptualization of the proposed architecture includes FL, blockchain anchoring, Explainable AI, Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and the prototype is implemented in FL simulation, blockchain logging, and model evaluation because of the available practical resources. Eight heterogeneous supply chain datasets were preprocessed and then given out to simulate multiple client training with FedAvg aggregation algorithm, and a Python based blockchain ledger was utilised to record immutable model updates. These findings indicate that the federated model is able to perform equally as a centralised baseline on non IID data and preserve privacy, and offer a verifiable audit trail. In general, the paper illustrates that decentralised AI is a viable solution to supply chain optimisation and provides a roadmap of the future development of the solution using sophisticated modelling elements and scalable implementation plans.

title: A Case Study of AI-Based Human-AI Collaboration in Reading Promotion within University Libraries
abstract: This study investigates the application of Generative AI (GenAI) in human-AI collaborative reading promotion within Chinese university libraries, addressing the paradigm shift from 'resource pushing' to 'demand response.' Utilizing a case study methodology, it analyzes practices from libraries including Harbin Institute of Physical Education, Shijiazhuang University, and Shenyang University of Technology to examine AI's role across the entire activity chain: planning, resource provision, service implementation, and effect evaluation. The research finds that mature collaboration models exhibit a three-dimensional structure of 'technology empowerment, librarian leadership, and reader co-creation,' where the organic integration of intelligent tools and professional expertise enhances service coverage and engagement. However, the study also identifies persistent challenges, including technical immaturity and data security risks. It concludes by proposing strategic countermeasures—such as optimized technology selection, specialized talent cultivation, and robust system construction—to provide a practical reference for advancing intelligent reading promotion in the academic library sector.

title: Convergence of Blockchain and Machine Learning for Intelligent Supply Chain Management: A Systematic Analysis of Synergies, Applications, and Emerging Trends

abstract: This extensive review analyzes 255 peer-reviewed articles (2020-2025) from the Scopus database to investigate the synergistic integration of blockchain and machine learning (ML) technologies in supply chain management (SCM).Our systematic review highlights five convergence themes at the core: (1) Immutable Traceability -blockchain-based decentralized ledgers ensure product path visibility and ML identifies supply chain data anomalies; (2) Intelligent Forecasting -ML-based algorithms drive demand forecasting and inventory optimization via blockchain-verified historical information; (3) Automated Compliance -smart contracts enforce business rules verified by ML-tested processes; (4) Sustainable Operationsblockchain records carbon footprint and ML optimizes resource usage and waste minimization; and (5) Cyber-Resilience -blockchain-based encryption protects IoT networks with ML-driven threat discovery.Industry-specific findings uncover revolutionary effects Agri-food supply chains achieve 20-30% waste reduction with blockchain origin tracking and ML spoilage forecasting, Pharmaceutical logistics accomplish 99.7% counterfeiting prevention through blockchain provenance tracking and ML pattern detection, Manufacturing demonstrates 25% maintenance cost savings through blockchain-component histories and ML failure prediction Implementation challenges are measured across the literature: scalability constraints impact 68% of real-time applications, integration costs stand at $2.4M on average for businesses, and skill gaps affect 82% of adoption efforts.Blockchain structures that are quantum-resistant, generative AI for supply chain planning, and standards across industries are among the priorities for future research.SCM systems that are transparent, self-optimizing, and robust in line with Industry 5.0 are made possible by this synergy.

title: GenAI-Driven Digital Twin Models for Real-Time Simulation of Edge Retail Infrastructure
abstract: The proliferation of edge computing in retail introduces significant complexity in managing distributed, heterogeneous infrastructure susceptible to dynamic demand fluctuations and disruptions. Traditional simulation and static digital twins (DTs) lack the adaptability and predictive fidelity required for proactive management. This research presents a novel framework integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) with Digital Twins to create dynamic, real-time simulation models of store-level edge retail infrastructure. We detail the architecture, leveraging Neural Operators, Temporal Graph Neural Networks (T-GNNs), and conditional diffusion models to synthesize high-fidelity system states, predict resource utilization under stochastic conditions, and generate plausible incident scenarios for resilience testing. Implemented using optimized model inference within Apache Flink streaming pipelines and validated against emulated edge environments, our GenAI-DT demonstrates a 32.7% improvement in forecasting accuracy (MAPE) and enables sub-second anomaly impact assessment, significantly enhancing proactive capacity planning and operational resilience. Key challenges around computational overhead and explainability are discussed, alongside future research directions in federated learning and meta-learning for self-evolution.

title: AI in Supply Chain Optimization
authors: Oscar Novak; Lea Popescu; Clara Popescu
abstract: Global supply chains operate under compounding uncertainty -- volatile demand, supplier disruptions, transportationdelays, geopolitical risk, and climate-related shocks -- that traditional operations research methods address throughdeterministic optimisation and scenario planning but cannot dynamically adapt to in real time. AI-powered supply chainoptimisation offers three capabilities traditional methods lack: demand forecasting that captures non-linear and causalrelationships in high-dimensional signals, real-time replanning under disruption, and autonomous decision support formulti-echelon inventory and routing optimisation. This study evaluates eight AI approaches for supply chain optimisationacross five problem domains: demand forecasting, inventory optimisation, supplier risk assessment, vehicle routing, anddisruption response. Methods include gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM), Temporal Fusion Transformer(TFT), deep reinforcement learning for inventory control (DRL-Inv), Graph Neural Networks for supplier risk (GNN-Risk),large language model-powered planning agents (LLM-SCM), combinatorial optimisation with neural heuristics(OR-Neural), and a hybrid ensemble. Data from 12 European manufacturing companies across six sectors (automotive,pharmaceutical, electronics, food, energy, and logistics) over 2019-2023 -- including the COVID-19 disruption period --was used for evaluation. TFT achieves the lowest demand forecasting MAPE (8.4%) across product categories. DRL-Invreduces inventory holding costs by 18.6% vs. EOQ baseline while maintaining service levels. GNN-Risk predicts supplierdisruptions 14.2 days earlier than human supply chain managers. LLM-SCM reduces disruption response time by 42.4%in simulation but introduces hallucination risks requiring human validation. A sector-specific AI adoption roadmap isproposed.

title: Large models in transportation infrastructure: a perspective
abstract: In late 2022, OpenAI launched ChatGPT and quickly came into the spotlight based on the development of large language modeling technology. ChatGPT is regarded as a new breakthrough in artificial intelligence technology, marking a major advancement in AI technology, stimulating global attention to the application of AI products, and opening up the ‘large model era’ of AI. Large models are also reshaping tasks and achieving impressive results in a wide range of complex downstream tasks (Li et al., 2023). The rapid development of large models provides new solution possibilities for the challenges faced by the transportation infrastructure industry. For the complicated industry specifications, design standards, feasibility study reports, and other textual data, large models can help them to study and integrate to better cope with the complex and changing application scenarios. At the same time, data management and analysis with the help of large language models in the era of big data can facilitate the study and formulation of data standards and processing procedures applicable to the transportation infrastructure industry and promote the scientific application of data in program decision-making and planning. Large models refer to deep neural network models with billions, tens of billions, or even more parameters (Lu, 2019). As shown in Fig. 1, such models are usually pre-trained on massive corpora and can learn complex patterns, linguistic nuances, and semantic relationships, but they are not targeted at a specific downstream task per se but rather gain an understanding of the training data. The application of large models means that the pre-trained large models are used to integrate and migrate the acquired knowledge to each specific downstream task through transfer learning. The training basis of large models The success of large models is inseparable from the application of its key technologies, such as self-attention mechanisms (Vaswani et al., 2017), self-supervised learning (Raffel et al., 2020), prompt engineering, etc. Transformer can model the context relationship in data (text, image, etc.) to obtain rich and effective data representation. Large language models, such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and GPT (Radford et al., 2018), are trained using the Transformer architecture. After the establishment of large models, their downstream applications are based on self-supervised learning. This learning mode avoids the mapping relationship between only fitting data and simple and highly abstract annotations in supervised pre-training and enables the model to learn data representations with rich semantic expression ability and strong generalization ability, so as to better transfer ‘knowledge’ to specific downstream tasks. Hint engineering is regarded as a catalyst to guide the model to output expected answers (Kirillov et al., 2023). Through well-designed inputs, the model can be guided to complete specific tasks, not only in text, but also in modalities, such as images. According to the training data and the type of modality output, large models can be mainly divided into language, visual, and multimodal large models. Language large models learn general features from massive texts, while visual large models focus on giving computers human-like visual processing abilities for understanding, identifying, and processing images and videos. Multimodal large models integrate multi-source data, such as text and images, which is the key to general artificial intelligence (AGI) (Blum and Blum, 2023), and have shown potential in biomedical (Li et al., 2023), scientific research (Beltagy et al., 2019), and other fields. The development of the GPT series models has heralded the era of large pre-trained language models. In addition to the GPT series, companies, such as Google and Microsoft, have also been continuously releasing large models with parameters ranging from hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions. Due to the high dependence of large models on massive computational power and data resources, the research forces are mainly from the industrial community. However, with the release of open-source large models of different parameter sizes by universities, such as Berkeley and Tsinghua, the academic community has also been able to actively participate with limited computational resources. This article summarizes the basic situations of the current mainstream 10 open-source large models, as shown in Table 1 (research time up to April 2024, arranged in ascending order of release time). Representative open source large models basic situation. Representative open source large models basic situation. As shown in Table 1, in the process of the development of open-source large models, the decoder architecture has dominated. The emergent abilities (i.e. abilities that are not explicitly programmed during training but are unexpectedly acquired, which can be understood as the creativity of large models) of the large models based on the decoder architecture with ‘big data + big parameters’ are also more pronounced, highlighting that large models with decoder architecture often possess stronger and more versatile performance. This paper provides a summary of the research status related to large models in the field of transportation infrastructure, as reported in publicly available research papers and patents. The study is organized into four stages: planning and design, project management, operation and maintenance, and safety control. As illustrated in Table 2, the number of literature related to the stage of safety control is the highest, followed by the stages of planning and design and project management. In contrast, the stage of operations and maintenance has the fewest number of literature. This distribution shows the hotspots and focal points of academic research at different stages, while it also highlights some area, particularly operations and maintenance, that may require more research attention, to ensure the overall success and long-term benefits of transportation infrastructure projects. These methodologies and models hold significant guidance and reference value for the establishment of specialized large models within the domain of transportation infrastructure. Literature on large models in transportation infrastructure industry. Literature on large models in transportation infrastructure industry. As depicted in Fig. 2, transportation infrastructure projects encompass a multitude of engineering data, industry standards, and local or national policies, the complexity of which necessitates interdisciplinary research to ensure successful integration (Uddin et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024). Moreover, the various stages of transportation infrastructure, from planning and design to construction and maintenance, demand a diverse array of specialized skills and knowledge. This integration process relies on the collaborative efforts of a multidisciplinary team comprising designers, engineers, and other professionals, presenting significant challenges for the research and development of large models in transportation infrastructure. The construction process of a large model for transportation infrastructure Large models hold the potential to play a pivotal role in design assistance and inspiration. By analyzing extensive datasets encompassing geographical and economic information (Roberts et al., 2023), these models can aid transportation infrastructure engineers in gaining a more profound understanding of the natural environment and socio-economic conditions of the project site, thereby facilitating the formulation of more rational plans. This is particularly crucial for applications involving environmental data, such as the alignment design of railways and highways, the site selection and planning of stations and bridges, and geospatial analysis, among others. Furthermore, large models can be integrated into the design process to generate design options and recommendations. By incorporating AI-based blueprint review technologies that have been developed over the years, it is possible to achieve intelligent interactions between large language models and engineering drawings (Chen et al., 2022). This capability can be utilized for understanding, querying, and manipulating various architectural domain data, including drawings, models, and specifications, thereby significantly enhancing the efficiency of project design communication. Large models are capable of conducting real-time analysis of various data throughout the project implementation process, thereby offering decision support for project management. Leveraging large language models can assist in the analysis of railway bid documents and the requirement analysis of railway-related software (Abbas et al., 2023; Bashir et al., 2023), which aids in advancing project progress and enhancing the efficiency of project completion. In the realm of operations and maintenance, a comprehensive perspective that considers the viewpoints of designers, civil engineers, and AI programmers can be employed. Utilizing large models for project planning, operational management, design enhancement, and risk mitigation (Rane, 2023) can foster collaboration, effective communication, and the integration of interdisciplinary expertise. In the context of safe control for transportation infrastructure, research on the application of large models mainly involves training and fine-tuning the base models using accident images and textual reports. For instance, by integrating GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) with stable diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), and incorporating relevant knowledge about foreign object intrusions on railways, high-quality and highly realistic samples of railway intrusion images can be generated, achieving the goal of preventing railway disasters (Chen et al., 2023). Alternatively, effective action plans can be rapidly generated by including disaster response and planning guidelines in the initial prompts (Goecks and Waytowich, 2023). Similarly, large models can be utilized to analyze aviation safety (Chandra et al., 2023) by mining accident sample data. Looking ahead, the development and research of large models for transportation infrastructure will not be confined to the current domain of professional knowledge querying but will also integrate multimodal technologies. By fine-tuning pre-trained large models toward the field of transportation infrastructure, there is an expectation to create an AIGC (AI-Generated Content) platform specific to this domain, aiming to achieve artificial substitution in engineering processes. Leveraging in-depth industry expertise and relying on AIGC technology, the planning and design of transportation infrastructure is anticipated to achieve intelligent breakthroughs at the forefront. In particular, preliminary design, which relies heavily on industry experience, requires the development of more sophisticated algorithmic models based on professional knowledge. This process entails a longer development cycle and is challenging to realize in the short term. Conversely, construction drawing design is relatively procedural, but it encompasses numerous specialized sub-fields that need to be tackled one by one. In the long term, as model algorithms continue to mature, large models are expected to become involved in various stages, including conceptualization, preliminary design, three-dimensional model output, and drawing review. This integration aims to establish a complete closed-loop system from ‘demand input’ to ‘AI design’, ‘demand feedback’, and ‘design updates’, thereby significantly enhancing design efficiency and optimizing business models. Furthermore, in the field of structural health monitoring, research related to large models barely exists. However, given the robust text data analysis capabilities of large models, there is potential for their application in real-time data analysis of sensors through training and fine-tuning. This could lead to the monitoring of the structural health conditions of transportation infrastructure. Taking the professional intelligent Q&A of railway line selection as a starting point, a professional knowledge Q&A platform case was constructed by combining a large model with a knowledge base to achieve the resolution of issues related to railway line selection. This application not only reflects the practical application value of large models in the field of transportation infrastructure but also demonstrates the potential of artificial intelligence technology in enhancing decision-making efficiency and accuracy. From the perspective of document processing, the working principle of the railway line selection knowledge Q&A platform is shown in Fig. 3. The realization principle of railway line selection knowledge Q&A The case study first examines the Langchain framework and its application in the construction of a professional knowledge base for railway line selection. By employing the data extraction methods of Langchain as well as text embedding techniques, a professional vector data knowledge base for railway lines is established. Subsequently, as shown in Fig. 4, a web-based intelligent Q&A platform for railway line selection is established. It integrates retrieval-enhanced generation technology, text embedding technology, semantic retrieval technology, and prompt engineering. The platform utilizes the BGE embedding model and the ChatGLM2-6B large language model and integrates them into the Q&A system, designing a user-friendly web interface. Langchain+LLM professional Q&A WebUI of railway route selection The case study uploads the document ‘TB 10098-2017 Code for Design of Railway Line’ as the knowledge file and poses questions regarding this specification. The responses obtained from the test are consistent with the content of the provisions recorded in the design specification, as shown in Fig. 5, and are not fabricated. Example of professional Q&A on railway line selection The case study illustrates the strengths of large models in the field of knowledge Q&A. By drawing on this example, knowledge-based Q&A platforms can be established for other specific segments within the field of transportation infrastructure. Looking further into the future, industry-specific algorithms can be integrated into the web platform for invocation, allowing for the modification of algorithm parameters through interaction with the large model. Additionally, a knowledge base can be constructed using engineering case data, enabling the large model to refer to the case database to make suggestions for new tasks. Despite the encouraging achievements made by artificial intelligence in the field of transportation infrastructure, the development of large models within this domain still faces significant challenges, with numerous technical difficulties and issues. The problems shown in Fig. 6 are particularly pronounced. Difficulties and Challenges in developing large models for transportation infrastructure The data within the transportation infrastructure domain encompasses a variety of document types, such as engineering technical forms and design drawings, which include both structured and unstructured elements. To effectively process such data, large models must comprehend their structure and the relationships among them. Documents in the transportation infrastructure field are typically lengthy. As document length increases, large models face challenges in locating key information segments and processing the internal semantic relationships within the documents. Concurrently, there is an urgent need to integrate specialized domain knowledge. The retrieval augmented generator (RAG) architecture (Lewis et al., 2020) is designed to address this challenge, but its integration with the transportation infrastructure context is currently insufficient. In the context of sensitive engineering and topographical information, data privacy protection and security precautions are critical issues for the use of large model technology in the transportation infrastructure sector. It is imperative to implement robust security measures, such as encrypted transmission and enhanced activity monitoring. Additionally, adherence to industry standards and regulations is essential to circumvent potential data privacy and security issues that may arise during the development and application of large models. Due to the nature of large models as black-box models, their internal decision-making processes are hardly interpretable. However, in the context of transportation infrastructure work, explaining the decision-making process of models is not only crucial for overall planning and architectural design stages but also essential for each phase of transportation infrastructure to comply with relevant standards and industry norms. Therefore, the interpretability of the model is equally important. Large models exhibit stability issues, where the model’s output may vary significantly in response to minor changes in the input data, potentially impacting the system’s reliability and consistency. Additionally, managing the connectivity and correlation between different tasks within transportation infrastructure projects represents a significant challenge for large models. Transportation infrastructure projects typically encompass multiple stages, such as pre-feasibility studies, feasibility studies, preliminary designs, and so on. However, large models often tend to provide direct answers, neglecting the records of previous steps and lacking comprehensive and effective explanations and reasoning regarding the future steps and their sequence. As the technology of large models rapidly advances and the quality of their generated content progressively approaches human-level performance, this poses challenges for model evaluation. Currently, the assessment of large models primarily revolves around evaluation metrics (for instance, BLEU and ROUGE are utilized to assess the model’s generative capabilities) and datasets for evaluation. However, in the field of transportation infrastructure, the development and application of large models are still in their infancy, and there is a particular lack of established indicator systems and organized datasets for evaluation. To realize the practical application of large models in transportation infrastructure, the research and development of reliable evaluation methods has become an urgent task. Finally, in the human-centered process of transportation infrastructure construction, decisions at each stage are made by human agents who assume corresponding technical responsibilities. However, with the application of AI technologies, such as large models in the field of transportation infrastructure, the decision-making process will introduce an element of ‘machine will’. Given the large model technology’s capabilities for continuous self-learning and evolution, its decision outcomes may become unpredictable, leading to potential inconsistencies between user intent and model output. In such cases, the attribution of decision-making responsibility and the mechanisms for accountability become complex and difficult to clearly define. The intelligentization of transportation infrastructure largely depends on the integration of diverse AI technologies. Large models, machine learning, deep learning, and big data analytics are all critical components in this field. They work in concert to enhance aspects, such as planning and design, project management, operations and maintenance, and safety control. The integration of large model technology paves the way for the construction of safer, more efficient, and more human-centered transportation infrastructure. The solutions to the difficulties and challenges discussed in Section 4 rely on these artificial intelligence technologies previously mentioned. This includes the standardized construction of professional datasets specific to the transportation infrastructure field, the development of more coherent long-text segmentation techniques, and the creation of more concise and efficient text vectorization technologies. Additionally, it involves the establishment of external information retrieval technologies, evaluation datasets, and assessment metrics. The integration of artificial intelligence technologies centered around large models is imperative. Finally, data privacy protection measures and multi-party accountability mechanisms urgently require enhancement and refinement. Looking ahead, to achieve enhanced specialization, robustness, and generalizability in dynamic, interference, and non-prior complex environments, transportation infrastructure large model technology must make leaps in several areas. These include the transition from purely machine learning models to structurally interpretable models, from offline learning to continuous autonomous learning, and from rote learning to associative inference. Efforts should be concentrated on promoting interdisciplinary innovative research between artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and cognitive science within the field of transportation infrastructure, striving to make breakthroughs in areas, such as interpretability, high security, and low power consumption.
